pages.query: 1000 wh power station bundled with a 400 w solar panel
pages.why_used: The rival pages give only rated Wh and their own 75–85% assumptions. None prints a named lab's delivered-energy figure for any of the 1 kWh kit stations. This page ranks the kits on lab-measured AC energy (BLUETTI AC180 980–1,030 Wh against 850–910 Wh for the EcoFlow, Jackery and Anker units) and adds the low-load result of 530–620 Wh at about 34 W.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the stations' 'max solar input' watts are not comparable: the BLUETTI AC180 is capped at 10 A, so its 2 × 200 W kit reaches 400 W only if the array runs at 40 V or more (series wiring). The Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2 drops to 8.2 A below 29 V, which allows about 230 W at most, and only Anker's 48 V PS400 panel gets the full 400 W through it, with its 57.6 V open-circuit voltage 2.4 V under the 60 V ceiling.
angles.decides: This confirms the pick rather than changing it. Each maker's own 400 W kit gets the whole 400 W (AC180 if wired in series, C1000 Gen 2 with the PS400). The finding matters for shoppers who would put a station together with panels bought separately: low-voltage 200 W panels in parallel lose about half their output on the AC180 (10 A cap) and on the C1000 Gen 2 (8.2 A below 29 V). On cycle life, Anker's '4,000 cycles to at least 80%' is the only figure from a maker page I read that names its endpoint. The ALLPOWERS P1800 (cheapest kit, $698) gives no endpoint and its rating differs between stores (US store: 'over 3,000'; a search snippet of the EU page says 3,500+), so the table footnote should say its cycle count can't be compared.

This page works those hours out from DashCamTalk's bitrates: about 7.2 h front + rear for the 70mai M800 and about 2.0 h for the DDPAI Z90 Master's eMMC. It also gives a DashCamTalk fill test of 4.1 h for the REDTIGER F77's 128 GB.

On DDPAI's Z90 line, the 64GB eMMC works together with a microSD card of up to 512GB under DDPAI's D²save "Dual-Storage System". I could not open a page showing which footage stays on the eMMC once a card is inserted.

A shopper who strictly wants no card at all is better matched by the 70mai M500 (eMMC only). The page should say in plain words that the DDPAI eMMC sits alongside a card and does not replace it.

With front and rear recording, the 70mai M800 holds about 7.3 h in its 128 GB, the REDTIGER F77 about 4.6 h in its 128 GB, and the DDPAI Z90 Master about 2.0 h in its 64 GB. pages.why_used: The cited B&H compare pages and Sweetwater grids repeat bare maker watt figures. The 1,500 W Behringer headline is its 2 Ω rating, and it gets set against Crown's 4 Ω rating with no rating conditions given for either. None of them says which rating states its test conditions, which one Audio Science Review measured at 268 W at 20 Hz, or that the Fosi M03's included 32 V brick limits it to about 128 W into 4 Ω. Angle A covers all four candidates. Angle E's bench data (standout 3, but no measurements of the Dayton or Fosi) is used as the evidence inside it.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got points out that the watt figures on these amps are measured under different conditions. Dayton rates the SPA250DSP at 250 W RMS into 4 Ω at under 0.1% THD+N. Behringer gives the NX3000D's 900 W/1,500 W per channel with no conditions at all. TI rates the TPA3255 chip at 10% THD+N (600 W) and only 480 W at 1%. The Fosi M03's own page gives 200 W RMS and 150 W RMS for the same 4 Ω load, and its 32 V/5 A power brick is rated 160 W, so it can't supply the 200 W spec.
angles.decides: This confirms the dedicated-amp picks but changes how to size them. Read the power figure at the sub's own impedance, and trust it only when the conditions are given. Dayton's 250 W into 4 Ω at under 0.1% THD+N is the only one of the three cards with stated conditions. The NX3000D's 900 W/ch into 4 Ω (not 1,500 W) has none, so treat it as headroom rather than a guaranteed continuous figure. For the Fosi M03 as shipped, size to the 150 W RMS into 4 Ω figure. That makes it a match for subs rated about 150 W or less. Getting near 200 W needs a stronger supply than the 32 V/5 A brick, within the 24–48 V input range.
products: general (TI TPA3255, the chip in the Fosi M03)

The 2 Ω-rated choices among the candidates are Fosi's own M01-BT (2–8 Ω) or the Behringer NX3000D (2 x 1,500 W at 2 Ω).
angles.decides: The pick depends on the sub's impedance. For a 4 Ω or 8 Ω passive home sub fed from an AVR's RCA sub out, the Fosi M03 works ($76.49, RCA in, 20–200 Hz low-pass), but Fosi says the supplied 32 V/5 A brick does not reach rated maximum power (DC input goes up to 48 V). For a 2 Ω load, rule out the M03 and the Dayton SPA250DSP (rated only into 4 Ω). Pick the Fosi M01-BT (2–8 Ω, $89.99) or the NX3000D in stereo mode (2 x 1,500 W at 2 Ω, $339). The NX3000D is rated down to 4 Ω when bridged. The Dayton SPA250DSP is a plate amp that needs a 9.25 x 6.25 in cutout in the sub's cabinet, so it only suits DIY enclosures you can cut. The Crown XLS 1002 is the only rack candidate whose maker page I opened that lists RCA inputs (alongside XLR and 1/4 in), so it connects directly to an AVR sub out.

angles.name: Mechanism
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that a class-D sub amp's output is capped by its supply voltage, so the Fosi Audio M03 cannot reach its rated power on the 32 V / 5 A brick it ships with: Fosi says 'you need a more powerful power supply to get the MAX power output', and the ideal ceiling at 32 V is about 128 W into 4 Ω and 64 W into 8 Ω, below its own 150–200 W (4 Ω) and 100–120 W (8 Ω) ratings.
angles.decides: For a home passive sub fed from an AV receiver's RCA sub out, the Fosi M03 is the only candidate here that takes RCA directly, has its own 20–300 Hz low-pass and costs under $100. Its real power, though, depends on the supply: plan on about 128 W at 4 Ω with the included 32 V brick and buy Fosi's 48 V supply to approach the rating (ideal ceiling about 288 W at 4 Ω). The sub must be 4–8 Ω. The Crown XLS 1002 also takes RCA. The Behringer NX3000D lists only XLR/TRS combo inputs, so it needs an RCA-to-XLR/TRS cable. The Dayton SPA250DSP is a plate amp that mounts in a 9.25 x 6.25 in cutout in the sub's own cabinet, so it only fits a DIY or modified box.

angles.name: Named measurements
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that Audio Science Review's bench test (amirm, 2020-07-06) measured the Behringer NX3000D at about 400 W per channel into 4 Ω, falling to 268 W at 20 Hz, against Behringer's 900 W rating. That is the amp ChatGPT ranked first as 'best value for powerful subs'. On the same test bench, the Crown XLS1002 went onto ASR's recommended list 'for driving subwoofers'.
angles.decides: This undercuts ChatGPT's top pick. At 20 Hz, where a passive sub needs the power, Amir measured the NX3000D at 268 W per channel, about 30% of its 900 W/ch 4 Ω rating. The same reviewer measured the Crown XLS1502 at about 336 W at 0.008% distortion. He recommended both the XLS1002 and the XLS1502 for subwoofer duty, and he faulted the NX3000D's fan for running at full speed from power-up. So the Crown is the better-sourced pick, and the NX3000D's '1,500 W' headline should not decide a purchase. I found no measurements for the Dayton SPA250DSP or the Fosi M03, so on this angle neither can be ranked against the rack amps.

pages.why_used: The rival buyer's guides (invenio3d, TriMech's SHINING 3D guide, 3D Scanner Match) give only headline single-figure accuracies, or no figures at all. None applies the base + rate × length volumetric formula to a real part size, and none says which maker names a test standard. This page works out the error at 300 mm and at 1 m for each scanner from sourced specs, so a shopper can go from their tolerance to a scanner.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got turns the scanners' stated volumetric accuracy into error over a real part length. At 1 m the EinScan Rigil's Laser HD spec (0.04 + 0.06 mm/m) works out to ±0.10 mm, and its IR Rapid spec (0.1 + 0.4 mm/m) to ±0.50 mm. The FreeScan UE Pro2 with photogrammetry (0.02 + 0.015 mm/m) works out to ±0.035 mm. That puts the Rigil's laser mode exactly at the '±0.1 mm mechanical fit' limit that ChatGPT's own filter offers, its IR mode far past it, and the UE Pro2 about 3× tighter.
angles.decides: This confirms the higher tier and sharpens the middle one. For parts around 1 m that need ±0.05 mm or better, only the UE Pro2 with photogrammetry meets it on its stated spec (±0.035 mm). The Rigil should only be recommended in Laser HD mode for ±0.1 mm work, and its IR Rapid mode (±0.30 mm at 500 mm) is shape-capture only. The budget picks (MetroX, MetroX Pro, Raptor, Raptor Pro) can only be placed once their mm/m figures come from the maker. Creality's US store pages publish no accuracy figure at all, so the page can't quote one from the store.

angles.name: Derive
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got turns a scanner's volumetric-accuracy formula (a mm + b mm/m) into the worst-case error on a part of a stated size; for example, the HandySCAN 3D PRO works out to 0.038 mm on a 300 mm part and 0.080 mm on a 1 m part, and the FreeScan UE Pro2 with photogrammetry to 0.035 mm on a 1 m part.
angles.decides: It confirms the step-up pick for large parts. Over 1 m, the FreeScan UE Pro2 with photogrammetry (0.035 mm) holds less than half the worst-case error of the HandySCAN 3D PRO without MaxSHOT (0.080 mm), even though their headline accuracies are about the same (0.02 mm vs 0.030 mm). For parts of about 300 mm or less, the two are within 0.014 mm of each other (0.0245 vs 0.038 mm). That difference matters only below a ±0.05 mm fit tolerance. The budget pick (MetroX vs Raptor) cannot be decided from this run, because their maker formulas could not be opened today (HTTP 429/404).

angles.name: Compatibility
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states which computers the budget picks need. Creality's CR-Scan Raptor manual lists macOS 11.7.7 or later on Apple M1/M2/M3 chips with 16 GB RAM, and on Windows 10/11 64-bit it suggests an i7 7th-gen CPU, an NVIDIA card with 6 GB VRAM and 16 GB RAM. Creality sells its Scan Bridge ($299) for the 'Sermoon S1 & Raptor Series' only, and Otter owners must buy a separate version.
angles.decides: For a Mac user, the Raptor is the budget pick that has a maker-documented Apple-silicon path (M1/M2/M3, 16 GB). For a Windows user, Creality suggests an NVIDIA GPU with at least 6 GB VRAM, which adds cost if the PC has integrated graphics. This confirms Raptor versus MetroX as the budget pair, but a full head-to-head needs MetroX's own requirements, which I could not open (see unsourced). On the Revopoint side, the maker's ball-plate listing says its Revo Metro measurement module is 'currently available only for MetroY Ultra and MetroY Ultra CMM models'. So a MetroX buyer gets no Revo Metro accuracy-verification software and should budget separately for inspection software.

angles.name: Mechanism
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the per-metre term in a handheld scanner's volumetric-accuracy spec is multiplied by the length of the object being scanned (Revopoint: 'L is the length of the object'). For a reverse-engineering part, the error to expect is therefore base + rate × part length: about 0.06 mm for MetroX vs 0.032 mm for MetroX Pro on a 300 mm part. Creaform measures its figure as sphere spacing on a calibrated length artefact; Revopoint gives no test conditions.
angles.decides: This lets the page turn the shopper's tolerance into a pick. With the claimed specs, a part up to about 300 mm can be held near ±0.03-0.04 mm by MetroX Pro (0.032 mm) or HandySCAN 3D PRO (0.038 mm). Standard MetroX at its originally published spec reaches 0.06 mm, which is fine for '±0.1 mm mechanical fit' but not '±0.05 mm precision'. At 1 m the gap widens: MetroX 0.13 mm, MetroX Pro 0.06 mm, HandySCAN PRO 0.08 mm, HandySCAN PRO with MaxSHOT 0.045 mm. On paper this favours MetroX Pro over standard MetroX for anyone at or below ±0.05 mm. It also tells larger-part buyers to add photogrammetry (MaxSHOT or Revopoint's Global Marker mode). One caution: only Creaform states how its figure is measured (sphere spacing on a calibrated length artefact). Revopoint's figure has no stated test method, so the two sets of numbers are not measured the same way.

None says the Raptor's 0.02 mm blue-laser mode always needs at least 4 markers in frame (CNC Kitchen), that 3D Printing Industry's Seal test hit trouble on symmetrical parts and had to add reference markers, or that Revopoint sells a marker-topper turntable for featureless objects. pages.query: best 40gbps nvme ssd enclosure that doesnt throttle on long transfers
pages.why_used: The cited rival pages give peak speeds, maker claims or general warnings about throttling. None of them collects the named long-run tests with duration, room temperature, held write rate and SSD temperature. Those tests are the D1 SSD Plus's 2,550–2,600 MB/s AJA loop and its 15-minute stress test at 30 °C, OWC's one-hour run with no speed drop, the CM642's clean 450 GB write, and the CM850, which had to lose its sleeve to finish. Together they answer 'doesn't throttle on long transfers' directly and cover most candidates.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got puts the long-copy rate next to the headline speed. Makers advertise 3,707–3,900 MB/s from short benchmarks. ASUS's own 30-minute claim for the PA40SU works out to about 1,644 MB/s. PCWorld's 450 GB write on the UGREEN CM642, ChatGPT's 'best for sustained transfers' pick, was slower than a couple of 20Gbps (about 2 GB/s) USB 3.2×2 SSDs, even though the enclosure 'never suffered any thermal related issues'.
angles.decides: The CM642 stays the pick for long copies, but for a narrower reason: in PCWorld's 450 GB test it finished without the thermal dropout that stopped the UGREEN CM850, not because it holds about 3.8 GB/s. On copies of hundreds of GB, the SSD's speed after its cache fills and the copy tool (PCWorld saw Explorer vs FastCopy differences on the PA40SU) limit speed more than the enclosure's fan does. The table should show three numbers for each enclosure: the maker's peak, the host-specific cap (Apple Silicon or Thunderbolt), and any long-copy figure. The footnote should say that a 'no throttle' long write lands around 1.6–2 GB/s.

angles.name: Derive
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that Windows' default 'Quick Removal' write-cache policy cut the UGREEN CM642's single-queue sequential write from 2,523.54 to 1,375.07 MB/s in cdrinfo's test. On 1 TB that is about 12.1 minutes instead of about 6.6, a slowdown that has nothing to do with heat.
angles.decides: The UGREEN CM642 pick stands; only its own figures change. angles.name: Mechanism
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got says that thermal throttling happens inside the SSD itself. The drive's own firmware drops to lower-power states once its composite temperature passes the drive's own thermal-management thresholds. The drive counts each of those events and the seconds spent in them in its standard NVMe health log (Thermal Management Temperature 1/2 transition count and total time). Comparing those counters before and after a long copy is how you tell real throttling from the SLC-cache slowdown that ChatGPT and itechguides could not separate.
angles.decides: This shifts the advice from which enclosure to which enclosure plus which SSD. No enclosure can switch off throttling. It can only keep the SSD under thresholds the SSD's maker sets, and on bus power it has a limited power budget. A Thunderbolt 4 port must supply at least 15 W to accessories, and a plain USB4 port is required to supply half that. That supports the fan model (UGREEN CM642) for multi-hundred-GB copies paired with an efficient Gen4 SSD rather than a Gen5 one. It also gives the page a test anyone can repeat, which rivals lack: log the drive's thermal-management counters during a long copy. If they don't move while speed drops, the cause is the SLC cache, not heat. Caveat: I did not confirm that every ASM2464PD enclosure passes the NVMe health log through to the host. One commenter saw a UGREEN CM850 show up as 'ASMT 2464 USB drive (UAS)' in USBView.

None of them says that both new decks have one shared record/play head and that their noise reduction works only on playback, so no tape they record carries Dolby encoding. Nor do they say that neither deck can record on metal tape, or that the vintage picks have separate record and playback heads with separate Dolby encode and decode circuits. That is the reason behind the 'buy new or buy vintage' split, and this page puts it into the table for six decks.

angles.name: Mechanism
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that how bright a laser looks equals its power times the eye's sensitivity at its wavelength. By the CIE 1988 photopic table, the eye's sensitivity is 0.710 at 520 nm and 0.885 at 532 nm (green) but 0.107 at 650 nm (red). That makes a green laser look about 6.6–8.3× brighter than a red laser of the same power. Because the laser class caps power (Class 2 at 1 mW, Class 3R at 5 mW), a green Class 3R laser can look about 5× brighter than a green Class 2 laser like the Klein 56074, and about 33× brighter than a 1 mW, 650 nm red Class 2 laser.
angles.decides: This confirms that the main pick should be a green Class 3R light (the US Wuben X5 3R or the US Olight ArkPro) for anyone who wants to point at things at a distance or in daylight. The arithmetic: the 5 mW Class 3R cap × 0.710 = 3.55 brightness-weighted mW. A Class 2 green like the Klein 56074 (<1 mW) gives under 0.71, and a 1 mW, 650 nm red Class 2 gives 0.107. So ChatGPT's 'Best for work' Klein 56074 has at most a fifth of a 3R laser's visible brightness, and its red budget picks (Hyper Tough, Coast PM50R, Fenix E06R, Klein 56040) are far dimmer still. The same arithmetic means a Class 1 green at the 0.39 mW our page lists for the Wuben X5 Class 1 (0.39 × 0.710 = 0.277) would still look about 2.6× brighter than a 1 mW, 650 nm red. That gives the X5 Class 1 a sourced reason to rank above red lasers for workplaces that ban Class 3R.

pages.query: best nas for streaming a flac music library with navidrome or plexamp
pages.why_used: The Plex, Navidrome and UGREEN pages shoppers see for this question say only 'very low resource usage' or 'CPU-intensive'. None of them turns any NAS's wattage into a yearly cost for a server that stays on all the time, and none warns that the makers test with different numbers of drives. This page converts each maker's access and hibernation watts into kWh and dollars per year and checks them against what reviewers measured with two drives.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the makers' disk-standby power figures can't be compared directly. Each maker tests differently: UGREEN measured the DXP2800 with one 2 TB HDD hibernating (5.24 W), QNAP measured the TS-264 with both bays full (18.288 W), and Synology (6.08 W) and Asustor (12.7 W) don't say which drives they used.
angles.decides: The finding supports the N100 UGREEN DXP2800 as the pick for an always-on Navidrome/Plexamp box. Its 5.24 W maker figure was measured with one 2 TB drive, and OCinside's two-HDD RAID 1 test came out at about 7 W idle (as reported by starryhope), so its low figure holds up with two drives. The QNAP TS-264 looks about 3x worse on paper (18.288 W against 6.08 W for the DS225+), but QNAP tested with both bays full and the others didn't, so part of that gap is the test, not the hardware. The page should show the spec-sheet numbers in one column and the footnoted conditions in the next, and should not rank on the raw figures. At the spec-sheet disk-standby figures, 24/7 use comes to about 46 kWh/yr (UGREEN), 53 kWh/yr (Synology), 111 kWh/yr (Asustor) and 160 kWh/yr (QNAP). That spread matters more than CPU speed for a FLAC server. Sonic Analysis needs x86 (Plex), which rules out the DH2300 and other ARM units for Plexamp's analysis features but doesn't choose between the four x86 units.

angles.name: Derive
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states what each candidate NAS costs to run as a 24/7 music server. Using the makers' own access and hibernation wattages at the EIA's August 2026 US residential rate of 18.16¢/kWh, with 4 h/day of drive access and 20 h/day hibernated, that comes to about $8/yr for the UGREEN DH2300, $11/yr for the DXP2800, $13/yr for the Synology DS225+, $23/yr for the Asustor AS5402T and $32/yr for the QNAP TS-264. The TS-264 draws more with its disks asleep (18.3 W) than the DXP2800 does while reading (16.38 W).
angles.decides: This backs ChatGPT's top pick, the DXP2800: it is the cheapest x86 box to run that can do Plexamp Sonic Analysis ($11.29/yr), and $1.27/yr cheaper than the DS225+. It weakens the TS-264, which costs about $20.67/yr more than the DXP2800 to run, or about $103 over 5 years, on top of a higher price. For a Navidrome-only shopper, the ARM DH2300 is cheapest overall: $239.99 plus about $40 of power over 5 years, against $389.99 plus about $56 for the DXP2800. It can't run Plex's Sonic Analysis.

pages.query: best nas to run pi-hole or adguard home plus a wireguard vpn for the house

With containers running, the drive-asleep figures (5.24 / 6.08 / 18.288 W) don't apply, because UGREEN itself says Docker containers and always-active databases block hibernation. The like-for-like figures are 16.38 W (DXP2800), 16.98 W (DS225+) and 29.086 W (TS-264). That works out to about 143 kWh, 149 kWh and 255 kWh a year. So the TS-264's built-in WireGuard costs about 111 kWh a year more than a DXP2800 running WireGuard in a container. The DS225+ has nearly the same power draw as the DXP2800, but its makers' page lists no M.2 slot, so containers can't be moved off the hard drives to let them sleep. Its VPN Server also has no WireGuard. Both points favour the DXP2800 or TS-264 for anyone who wants the drives to sleep. Also normalised: native WireGuard on the stock OS. QNAP QVPN: yes (QNAP's own page). Synology DSM VPN Server: no (OpenVPN, L2TP/IPsec, PPTP only). UGREEN UGOS Pro: OpenVPN and WireGuard according to VPN Tracker only; no UGREEN page found.

One caution that is my own inference, not something a source said: the DS225+ has no NVMe storage pool (racksandwatts spec list), so Pi-hole or AdGuard containers would sit on the hard drives. Constant query logging could then stop the disks from sleeping, which moves it toward its 16.98 W access figure (about $27 a year). The DXP2800 can keep containers on NVMe.

On the QNAP TS-264 the same protection exists only after a switch from QTS to QuTS hero h6, and then deleting a protected folder needs a Secure Deletion USB key. On Asustor, TerraMaster and UGREEN, a 'locked' snapshot is only skipped by automatic cleanup and can still be deleted by hand. pages.why_used: Shoppers asking for a quiet gaming controller need to know which buttons are actually silenced. The cited rivals don't say: HLPLANET's G7 page only labels face buttons 'Membrane (Quiet/Soft)', and the Reddit threads and Super Nova manual carry owner opinion or bare specs. None goes input by input through what each maker's 'quiet' covers. None quotes EasySMX's own 'tactile microswitch' D-pad wording for the X05 Pro, and none sets out that the Chitu 2 Silent Edition swaps every button and the stick rings to silicone.

angles.decides: This confirms the X05 Pro as a pick but corrects what it is quiet at. The only named reviewer, Ban at Retro Handhelds, calls the D-pad 'a really quiet clicky', not silent. For D-pad-heavy play (platformers, fighting games), the Super Nova is the safer quiet choice on the makers' own specs: GameSir lists a membrane D-pad and The SixthAxis says the buttons are membrane 'across the board, including the D-pad'. Its quiet claim, though, covers ABXY only. Zowietek's own knowledge base says a 4K60 (console or PC) source is recorded at 1080p60. Only ClonerAlliance's UHD Pro page states it records a 4K60 source at 4K30, and no rival puts each recorder's 4K60-source result, top bitrate and hours per card side by side. Of the listed recorders that take 4K60 in, only the ClonerAlliance UHD Pro and UHD Pro Max state they record that source in 4K (4K30).

At their top bitrates a 128 GB card holds about 5.7 h (UHD Pro, UHD Pro Max and ZowieREC at 50 Mbps), 9.5 h (RecDual at 30 Mbps) or 14.2 h (HD PVR Pro 60 at 20 Mbps).

Buyers who need 4K pay in storage: at 50 Mbps a 4K30 recorder (UHD Pro, ZowieREC) fills a 256 GB card in about 11 h, roughly 4.5 GB per hour. For unattended or scheduled long recordings, a 1080p unit or a lower bitrate setting is the better fit: the ZowieREC's 12 Mbps default gives about 47 h per 256 GB, and the UHD Pro's 8 Mbps minimum about 71 h. The page should add one line telling shoppers to plan on a 1 TB+ USB drive for multi-day 4K recording.

pages.query: best triple-screen laptop extender for a 16-inch laptop with 19201200 panels
pages.why_used: The cited roundups and answers repeat the warning that base M1/M2 Macs support only one external display, and they offer driver-based extenders as the fix. None of them says that every Apple-silicon 16-inch MacBook Pro drives at least two external displays natively. None says that the USB-graphics drivers behind 'driver required' units block protected video on every screen. This page adds Apple's display counts per chip, FOPO's own driver and Mac statements, and Plugable's HDCP documentation.

angles.decides: For a 16-inch MacBook Pro (M5 Pro: 3 external displays; M5 Max: 4), the driver-free dual-16-inch extenders work with both screens extended and no driver. These are the FOPO S11 at $399.99 and the INVZI MagHub Dual Lite. That removes the Mac reason our page gives for picking the driver-based S788. The S788 is still the choice only for a buyer who wants three added screens, which makes four displays in total, not a triple-screen setup. For a laptop + 2 'triple' setup, the pick shifts toward the S11 or Dual Lite. The footnote for the table is: 'Triple' in product names is not a fixed count. FOPO S11 means laptop + 2 screens. FOPO S788 'Triple' means 3 added screens, so 4 displays. INVZI MagHub 'Quad Max' means 3 added screens.

angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that every 16-inch Apple-silicon MacBook Pro natively drives at least two external displays, so base-chip workarounds don't apply to a 16-inch Mac, or that the USB-graphics drivers behind 'driver required' extenders (DisplayLink, Silicon Motion InstantView) block HDCP-protected video such as Netflix and Prime Video on every screen of the Mac, including the built-in one, while they are connected.
angles.decides: For a 16-inch MacBook Pro, the Mac caveat that pushed ChatGPT toward driver-based extenders doesn't apply. The 2021 M1 Pro already drives two external displays natively, and the current M5 Pro drives three. So a driver-free two-screen extender is the pick, as long as each screen gets its own native video output: the INVZI MagHub Dual Lite (USB-C plus mini-HDMI per its Best Buy listing title) or the FOPO S11. Driver-based units (FOPO S788, MagHub Trio 'Driver Required') add a third screen. On a Mac they cost you protected streaming on all screens, and on macOS 15 and later the Screen Recording permission they need may have to be renewed periodically. Only someone who needs three external screens, or has a laptop without two video-capable outputs, should take that trade.

The sum: a USB 3.x SSD can draw up to 0.9 A, and a keyboard and mouse at one USB 2.0 unit load each add 0.2 A, so the three need 1.1 A (5.5 W). ATEN in fact requires a 5 V 3 A host. The old 'forward UDP 19132' setup therefore stops working: you now need TCP 19132 for signaling plus a range of UDP ports with one port per player (or TCP+UDP on 19132 for Geyser). playit.gg also says Bedrock Dedicated Server 'can't connect to playit by itself', so it needs a WaterdogPE proxy.
angles.decides: This doesn't change which NAS wins, because the transport works the same on any x86 Docker NAS (DXP2800, DXP4800 Plus, TS-464, DS925+). It does decide whether the shopper's plan works if any friend plays Bedrock (phone, Windows, console via Geyser). Two setups now work. (1) A Java server (itzg/minecraft-server, TCP 25565) plus Geyser build 1237 or later with transport set to nethernet, and 19132 open on both TCP and UDP. On Docker, Geyser also needs -DgeyserAdvertiseAddresses, because GeyserMC says it is for servers 'in containers or behind a NAT'. (2) Bedrock Dedicated Server with TCP 19132, a UDP range of at least max-players ports (default 10) and the public IP set in SERVER_UDP_PORTS. On playit.gg, that means adding WaterdogPE with online-mode=false. Either way the page should keep the 'Java server + Geyser on an x86 NAS' route as the main recommendation and correct the Bedrock port row.

pages.query: which kvm switch holds 4k 144 hz between a macbook pro and a gaming pc on one monitor
pages.why_used: The cited TESmart and Level1Techs pages only tell Mac buyers to 'confirm the external-display limits of the exact Mac model', or to use a USB-C-to-DisplayPort cable. None of them gives Apple's limits for each port. This page now does, from Apple's own documents: on M2 Pro to M4 Max MacBook Pros, 4K 144 Hz is rated only on the HDMI port and Thunderbolt only to 6K 60 Hz. The M1 Pro/Max HDMI port is limited to 4K 60 Hz, and only the M5 Pro/Max and M6 are rated for 4K 144 Hz on any port. That splits buyers between the HDMI route and the USB-C-to-DP route those pages recommend, and it corrects our old top row, which put the Mac on the monitor's USB-C.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that Apple rates the M2 Pro to M4 Max MacBook Pros for 4K above 60 Hz only on their HDMI port, with Thunderbolt listed at 6K 60 Hz. The same results also don't state that every DP 1.4 '4K144' claim needs DSC because 4K144 at 8-bit RGB carries 28.67 Gb/s of active pixels against DP 1.4's 25.92 Gb/s payload. Together these favour an HDMI 2.1 KVM over the USB-C-to-DisplayPort route ChatGPT and Level1Techs suggest.
angles.decides: The pick now depends on which Mac the shopper has. With an M2 Pro, M3 Pro or M4 Pro/Max MacBook Pro, the only port Apple rates for 4K above 60 Hz is HDMI. So an HDMI 2.1 KVM whose maker lists a 4K high-refresh mode is the sourced path: the TESmart HDK202-M24 lists 'Dual 4K@144Hz/160Hz (DSC 1.2a)', and the HKS201-M24 lists 4K240 (DSC). A DP 1.4 KVM fed by USB-C-to-DP (Level1Techs, TESmart DKS202-M24) has no Apple 4K144 rating on those Macs and needs DSC at 4K144 in any case. With a 2021 M1 Pro/Max, an HDMI KVM caps the Mac at 4K60. M5 Pro/Max is rated for 4K144 over Thunderbolt or HDMI, so either KVM type is possible. The current page's 'use the monitor's KVM' advice still holds, because a direct HDMI cable avoids the middle device, and Apple says to 'Connect displays directly to your Mac for best results'.
products: Level1Techs DP 1.4 KVM single monitor two computer

angles.name: Derive
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states the arithmetic: uncompressed 4K at 144 Hz and 8-bit colour needs 31.35 Gb/s, which is 121% of the 25.92 Gb/s a DisplayPort 1.4 (HBR3) KVM can carry (151% at 10-bit). 4K at 120 Hz and 8-bit fills 99.6% of that link. So every DP 1.4 KVM's '4K144' claim depends on DSC, while an HDMI 2.1 48G link carries 4K144 at 10-bit uncompressed at 93% of its 42.0 Gb/s.
angles.decides: On a DP 1.4 KVM (Level1Techs, TESmart DKS202-M24, StarTech D86A2, UGREEN 25962), 4K144 only works if DSC works end to end, Mac included. That is the very part ChatGPT kept telling the shopper to 'verify'. The finding favours connecting a MacBook Pro (M2 Pro/Max or later) from its own HDMI port, with no adapter, to an HDMI 2.1 48G KVM. That link has the headroom for 4K144 without compression. One catch: TESmart's HKS201-M24 page lists 4K144/165 as running 'through DSC' and makes no Mac claim, so no switch is proven to carry 4K144 uncompressed. This supports the current page's lead pick (use the monitor's built-in KVM, a direct link with no DSC middleman). It does not overturn it.
products: Level1Techs DP 1.4 KVM Single Monitor Two Computer

angles.name: Compatibility
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states which MacBook Pro chips can send 4K 144 Hz into an HDMI 2.1 KVM. Apple's own spec pages limit the HDMI port to 4K 60 Hz on the 2021 M1 Pro MacBook Pro and to 4K 120 Hz on the base M3 (Nov 2023). The M2 Pro (2023) and later reach 4K 240 Hz. Apple also says adapters aren't supported at those HDMI rates, so the Mac's own HDMI port has to go straight into the switch.
angles.decides: The Mac's chip decides the switch type. With an M2 Pro/Max (2023) or later, base M4/M5/M6, or M3/M4/M5 Pro/Max, the Mac's built-in HDMI port can feed an HDMI 2.1 KVM such as the TESmart HKS201-M24 at 4K 144 Hz alongside the PC. It must be a direct HDMI cable, not a USB-C-to-HDMI adapter. With an M1 Pro/Max or base M3 MacBook Pro, the HDMI side stops at 4K 60 Hz or 4K 120 Hz. Those Macs need the USB-C DP Alt Mode route into a DisplayPort KVM, using a DP Alt Mode USB-C-to-DP cable (Cable Matters says its switch 'is not natively compatible with computers with a USB-C port'). On that route, 4K 144 Hz depends on DSC working end to end (Cable Matters FAQ; L1Techs FAQ: 'Without DSC, no'), and Level1Techs officially rates its switch only to 4K 120 Hz. This keeps our page's verdict of using the monitor's built-in KVM for M1 Pro and base M3 owners, and it allows an HDMI 2.1 KVM for M2 Pro and later.
products: Apple MacBook Pro (M6 / M5 Pro / M5 Max, current)
Level1Techs DP 1.4 KVM Single Monitor Two Computer

angles.name: Mechanism
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states Apple's per-port limits. For MacBook Pros with M2 Pro/Max, M3 Pro/Max and M4/M4 Pro/M4 Max, Apple documents 4K at 144 Hz only on the HDMI port, and lists the Thunderbolt/USB-C ports at 6K 60 Hz. The 2021 M1 Pro/Max tops out at 4K 60 Hz on HDMI. Only the current M5 Pro/Max and M6 models list 4K 144 Hz or more over any combination of Thunderbolt and HDMI.
angles.decides: For an M2 Pro through M4 MacBook Pro, the only Apple-documented 4K 144 Hz output is the HDMI port. So the Mac's side of the switch should be HDMI 2.1, either through an HDMI 2.1 KVM such as the TESmart HKS201-M24 or into the monitor's own HDMI 2.1 input when using the monitor's KVM, with the PC on DisplayPort. A DP 1.4 KVM such as the Level1Techs depends on a USB-C-to-DP plus DSC path that Apple does not document for those chips. On top of that, Level1Techs' own spec is 4K 120 Hz, with 144 Hz only through DSC. This also corrects our current top row. It puts the Mac on the monitor's USB-C (DP Alt Mode), which Apple documents only to 6K 60 Hz on these chips, so the Mac should go on the monitor's HDMI 2.1 input instead. For an M1 Pro/Max (2021), Apple documents no 4K 144 Hz output at all, so no switch fixes it. For the M5 Pro/Max and M6, Apple lists 4K 144 Hz or more on any port, including Thunderbolt, so DP and USB-C paths are documented too.

None of them sets the P2S, the CORE One+ and a QIDI side by side by how the chamber is actually heated. This page shows that at $449 the QIDI Q2 has a dedicated 280 W heater rated to 65 °C. pages.why_used: The cited Schumacher and Advance Auto pages and the top roundups put a plug-in combo's 100–200 A engine start next to a pack's 1,000 A or more peak. None of them says these are different kinds of rating. This page explains the plug-in figure: it is a capped current from the wall, limited to 7 seconds per crank and under 3 seconds on a hard crank, with a 180 s cool-down after repeated cranks, and it needs a battery installed in the car. It then compares that with the pack combos that jump-start without an outlet.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that Schumacher's plug-in 'engine start' amps are not the same kind of rating as a lithium pack's 'peak amps'. The SC1281/SC1309 rate is a capped current fed from the wall. It flows for up to 7 seconds per crank, and if the starter draws more than that rate the crank can last less than 3 seconds. Repeated cranks then trigger a 3-minute cool-down. A pack's '1,000 A peak' is a brief maximum, so 100 A vs 1,000 A is not a 10× difference in starting power.
angles.decides: This confirms that the plug-in Schumacher combos (SC1281 at 100 A, SC1309 at 200 A) suit a shopper who has an outlet and time. The charger gives a capped, timed boost with a 2-minute wait before cranking, and on a hard-to-turn engine the crank can drop below 3 seconds. A shopper who needs a strong start away from an outlet should not choose by comparing the 100 A or 200 A figure with a pack's peak amps. They should choose a lithium pack or a pack-plus-charger unit such as the Battery Tender CNS 4120. The page should footnote the amp column as 'charger engine-start rate (AC, capped, 7-second crank) vs pack peak (instantaneous)'.

angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got gives hours to recharge: Schumacher's own manual chart says a 6 A combo like the SC1281 or SC1309 needs 10 h to refill a half-flat 1000 CCA truck battery and 4 h for a 300 CCA car battery (30 h and 12 h on the 2 A maintain rate), and a 10 A timer-wheeled unit like the SC1446 delivers at most 22.5 Ah per full 135-minute timer turn.
angles.decides: This confirms rather than overturns ChatGPT's picks. Every plug-in combo it showed charges at 6 A, so all of them refill a battery equally slowly, about 10 h for a large truck battery. They differ only in engine-start amps and price, so the shopper should choose on cranking amps (100 A for cars, 150–200 A for trucks) rather than expect any of them to charge faster. If faster recharging matters, a 10 A unit cuts the 1000 CCA case to 7 h, but the manual-timer wheeled models (SC1446, SC1667) need the 135-minute timer reset about 4 times to get there. A shopper who wants a hands-off overnight recharge should pick an automatic 6 A unit (SC1281L or SC1309) over a timer-wheeled one.

pages.why_used: The cited rivals each print half of the picture. Charge-Test gives XTAR's measured energy and Light And Matter gives EBL's, but neither sets measured energy next to the label. So nobody shows that the 38% label lead the XTAR 4150 has over the EBL 3000 shrinks to 0.5–4.5% when measured, that the EBL beats its own label while the XTARs reach 82–86% of theirs, or that the label that looks biggest (PUJIMAX 4,255 mWh) measured the least. The page also adds Gough Lui's mAh × voltage check, which explains the gap, and his cycle-wear test, which Charge-Test says it did not do.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that once you swap printed ratings for measured energy, the 38% capacity lead the XTAR 4150 mWh AA has over the EBL 3000 mWh AA on the label shrinks to roughly 0.5–4.5%: XTAR measured 3,420 mWh (82% of its rating) and EBL measured 3,273–3,404 mWh (109–113% of its rating).
angles.decides: ChatGPT called the XTAR 4150 'best overall' for 'high capacity' and the EBL 3000 mWh 'budget'. On measured energy the two are close: within about 5%, or 6–11% if you use XTAR's own 0.25 A figure (3,605 mWh). So the pick between them should rest on price per pack, charger fit and high-current behaviour, not on the mWh printed on the label. The XTAR CLR 4300 is still the measured capacity leader at 3,703 mWh. Its lead shrinks at high drain: about 2,300–2,440 mAh at 2 A against 2,676 mAh at 1 A. Caveat: the XTAR and EBL figures come from different test rigs (charge-test averaged 0.1/0.4/1 A; Light And Matter used an XTAR VX4 V2 with no current stated). This is directional, not a head-to-head test.

angles.decides: This confirms the XTAR CLR 4300 as the pick on value as well as capacity, and it challenges ChatGPT's 'budget' label for the EBL: at the maker stores the EBL costs about 30% more per measured Wh than the CLR 4300 (4-pack against 4-pack: $2.36 vs $1.82). angles.name: Mechanism
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that XTAR's 1.5 V AA cells have their own charge-management chip and take 4.75–5.5 V only from a charger that supports XTAR's 1.5 V Li-ion protocol. That means a NiMH charger won't do it, and XTAR's own store says its VX4 V1 charger cannot charge the CLR 4300 that ChatGPT made its top pick.
angles.decides: This confirms the XTAR CLR 4300 as the pick only if it's bought with a charger XTAR lists as compatible: the L4 Pro, MX4, L4 or L8, or a VX4 V2 but not a V1. The cheapest sure route is XTAR's USA L4 Pro + 4× CLR 4300 bundle at $39.99, against $26.99 for the batteries alone. Someone who already owns a NiMH charger, such as the Tenergy TN480U that Dealectric lists, can't charge these cells with it. The same mechanism explains each candidate's low-battery behaviour: the EBL holds 1.5 V and then cuts off, the XTAR 4150 steps down to 1.1 V, and the CLR 4300 declines linearly to about 1.0 V. In devices that judge charge by voltage, only the stepped and sloped designs give a warning before the device dies.

None of them works out how many peak-sun hours each kit's own panels need to refill its own battery, and none compares that across brands. That figure is what shows the 6.5 kW SGM-6510M (4.6 h) and Renogy's 400 W kit (9 h) can't refill in one day, while the $4,949 SGR-8K10E refills in 2.8 h. pages.why_used: The cited rival pages give inverter output only in VA or W. I opened Solar Waypoint, PluginSolarCheck, Solar United Neighbors and APsystems' pages, and none of them converts those ratings to amps on the house circuit. None checks the totals against the EZ1-LV's dedicated 10 A circuit condition or works out how much current breaker masking can let through. None points out that APsystems' own claim of '2 units on a standard 15A circuit' (15 A) is more than that condition allows. This page adds the current figures from the makers and retailers, the arithmetic, Hoymiles' plug and shutdown timings, and the CEC efficiencies.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got turns the VA ratings into amps on the house circuit: APsystems EZ1-LV 900 VA = 7.5 A and Hoymiles HiFlow Pro LV 360–500 VA = 3.0–4.17 A, so one EZ1 uses 75% of the 10 A dedicated circuit that rivals cite as its install condition, and the two-unit '1,800 W on a standard 15A circuit' setup on APsystems' own consumer page adds 15 A, the full rating of a 15 A circuit.
angles.decides: This confirms the EZ1-LV as the two-panel pick, but only as a single unit: one unit at 7.5 A fits a 10 A dedicated circuit, while two units add 15 A. For a shopper who can't add a dedicated circuit, the HiFlow Pro LV adds only 3.0–4.17 A per unit. That makes it the low-load choice for one panel, which ChatGPT's 'budget' label doesn't explain.

angles.name: Derive
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got gives each inverter's yearly output in kWh or its price per yearly kWh. In NREL PVWatts v8 for Kansas City, a 900 VA APsystems EZ1-LV with matched panels makes about 1,288 kWh a year at a 20° tilt and about 865 kWh hung flat (vertical) on a balcony. That works out to $0.25 to $0.38 of inverter price per yearly kWh. A 360 VA Hoymiles HiFlow Pro LV makes about 515 kWh (20° tilt) or 346 kWh (vertical), which is $0.31 to $0.46 per yearly kWh.
angles.decides: This supports ChatGPT's pick of the EZ1-LV. It gives 2.5× the yearly energy of a 360 VA HiFlow Pro LV (1,288 vs 515 kWh) at a lower inverter cost per yearly kWh ($0.25 vs $0.31). At the US average rate that is about $234 vs $94 a year. It also matters for balcony buyers: hanging the panels vertically cuts yearly output by about a third. From November to January, though, a vertical array makes more than one at 20° (December: 98.4 vs 80.6 kWh per kW), so railing mounts lose mostly in summer. Caveats: the APsystems page carries a 5-unit order limit, and two rival pages say the EZ1-LV is sold out. I could not source the EcoFlow STREAM's AC rating, so it is left out of the comparison.

angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states which solar panels each plug-in microinverter can take: the APsystems EZ1-LV accepts 18 A per input across two inputs (25 A short-circuit) with a 27–45 V tracking range and recommended 315–660+ Wp modules, while each Hoymiles HiFlow Pro LV takes one module at 14–16 A and 64 V max, so a large modern panel above 14 A fits the EZ1-LV but is current-limited on the smaller HiFlow models.
angles.decides: This supports ChatGPT's EZ1-LV pick for a two-panel build. It is the only candidate with two 18 A inputs and a published 315–660+ Wp module range, so one unit can run two current large-format panels. The HiFlow Pro LV is one panel per unit, and the model has to match the panel: the 360/391/420 models allow 14 A, the 450 allows 15 A and the 500 allows 16 A. A shopper pairing a high-current panel with the $149 HMS-360 would lose output. Panels must stay under the 60–64 V input ceiling. That rules out series-wiring two panels into one input, and it rules out high-voltage rooftop strings.

angles.name: Mechanism
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got works out the breaker-masking current. A plug-in inverter's output goes onto the branch wiring without passing through the breaker, so one APsystems EZ1-LV (7.5 A nominal) on a shared 15 A circuit can let part of that wiring carry up to 22.5 A without tripping. APsystems' own consumer page still advertises two EZ1s, 1,800 W or 15 A, 'on a standard 15A circuit', while the CSA UL 3700 conditions reported by Solar Waypoint and Plugin Solar Check allow only a dedicated 10 A circuit. The Hoymiles HiFlow Pro LV adds only 3.0 A (360 VA model) and drops its plug to 34 V or less within 1 second of unplugging.
angles.decides: Confirms the EZ1-LV for one unit on its own dedicated circuit: 7.5 A fits a 10 A circuit. It rules out ChatGPT's implied path of stacking two EZ1s for 1,800 W on an ordinary shared 15 A outlet, because 15 A of backfeed exceeds the certificate's 10 A dedicated-circuit condition. For a shopper who must use a shared outlet, the Hoymiles HiFlow Pro LV is the safer pick: it adds 3.0 to about 4.2 A per unit, plugs into a GFCI outlet, and its plug goes dead within 1 s. Either way, the deciding question is which circuit the outlet is on, not the inverter's VA rating.

pages.why_used: The cited RV Upgrade Store page lists the 104 V / 132 V cutoff only for the EPO model. No cited page says the cheaper non-EPO Gen II only alerts and does not disconnect, or that both take the same RSM30W surge module. angles.decides: For a whole-RV smart device, the cheaper Gen II PWD30W is a surge protector with a monitor and alerts: it doesn't disconnect the RV in a brownout or when voltage runs high. pages.why_used: The cited roundups (Tech Advisor, and the 'up to 12 days' vs 'around one day' cards) give only whole-watch battery claims. None puts the makers' own GPS-workout hours on one footing, notes that the Venu 4 falls to 9 h (45 mm) / 6 h (41 mm) with all satellites plus music, or shows that Amazfit's under-$300 watches rate 33-64 h of GPS against Garmin's 20 h and Apple's 10 h. Angle A had the highest standout (3), and every figure in it now has a source.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states the makers' own continuous-GPS workout hours side by side: Apple Watch Series 12 up to 10 h, Apple Watch SE 3 up to 7 h, Fitbit Versa 4 up to 12 h, Garmin Venu 4 up to 15 h (41 mm) / 20 h (45 mm) in GPS-only mode but only 6 h / 9 h with all satellites plus music, while Samsung and Google publish no GPS-hours figure at all for the Galaxy Watch8 and Pixel Watch 4.
angles.decides: It confirms Garmin Venu 4 as the pick for long GPS sessions only in the 45 mm size and only in GPS-only mode (20 h); the 41 mm in all-satellite + multi-band + music mode (6 h) is shorter than an Apple Watch Series 12 outdoor run (10 h) and a Fitbit Versa 4 (12 h). For a shopper doing sub-2-hour workouts, the 10-day vs 1-day gap is about charging habit, not whether a workout gets tracked, so the Apple Watch Series 12 at $399 and the Versa 4 are fully competitive. Galaxy Watch8 and Pixel Watch 4 cannot be placed on this scale from maker data.

angles.name: Derive
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states how many days a fitness smartwatch lasts when you actually run with GPS for an hour every day: Garmin Venu 4 45 mm works out to about 7.7 days per charge at that duty cycle (6.2 days for the 41 mm), against 1.0 day for Apple Watch Series 12 and 0.75 day for Apple Watch SE 3, computed from the makers' own smartwatch-mode and GPS-mode ratings.
angles.decides: Confirms Garmin Venu 4 as the fitness pick but changes the advice inside it: a daily GPS runner should buy the 45 mm (7.7 days between charges, 20 one-hour GPS runs per charge) over the 41 mm (6.2 days, 15 runs). It also shows the Apple watches are strictly charge-every-night devices under a daily-workout cycle: Series 12 covers 10 one-hour GPS workouts per charge, SE 3 only 7, so on a run-every-day schedule Apple's 'all-day' claim is exactly one day with no slack. Samsung Galaxy Watch8 cannot be placed on this scale because Samsung publishes no GPS-mode hours.

angles.name: Compatibility
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states the makers' phone floors: Apple Watch Series 12 / SE 3 require an iPhone 11 or later on iOS 27, Galaxy Watch8 requires Android 12 with 1.5 GB RAM and cannot pair to an iPhone at all, Pixel Watch 4 requires Android 11 with no iPhone support, and Samsung's ECG/blood-pressure features require a Galaxy phone, a user aged 22+, and a cuff recalibration every 28 days.
angles.decides: Confirms ChatGPT's split (Apple for iPhone, Samsung/Pixel for Android, Garmin/Fitbit for either) but adds the hard exclusions: a shopper on an iPhone X/XS or older, or on iOS 26, cannot pair the Apple Watch Series 12 or SE 3 that ChatGPT recommended; an iPhone owner cannot use the Galaxy Watch8 or Pixel Watch 4 at all; an Android phone below Android 12 (Samsung) or Android 11 (Google) is excluded; and a non-Samsung Android owner buying the Galaxy Watch8 loses ECG, blood pressure and sleep coaching, which moves them toward the Pixel Watch 4 or Garmin Venu 4. Garmin's ECG is region-limited and 22+ only, so the Venu 4's 'works with both phones' advantage does not extend to ECG everywhere.

angles.name: Mechanism
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states the pairing mechanism in the makers' own words: Samsung's compatibility table lists iOS as 'Not supported' for the Galaxy Watch8 series (Android 12.0 or higher, 1.5 GB RAM), Apple requires iPhone 11 or later on iOS 27 for Series 12 / SE 3, and Garmin's manual says text replies are 'available only for compatible Android phones' because the phone, not the watch, sends the SMS, so a Garmin Venu 4 on an iPhone shows texts but cannot answer them.
angles.decides: The phone in the shopper's pocket decides the shortlist before any fitness metric does. iPhone owners: Galaxy Watch8/Watch9 and Pixel Watch are out (Samsung: iOS 'Not supported'); Apple Watch SE 3 / Series 12 need iPhone 11+ on iOS 27; Garmin Venu 4 (and Lily 2 Active) and Amazfit pair fine but cannot reply to texts from the wrist. Android owners: Apple Watch is out; Galaxy Watch8 needs Android 12.0+ with 1.5 GB RAM, and blood pressure needs Android 12+ / Wear OS 4.0 with ECG tied to a Galaxy phone via the Galaxy Wearable app. This confirms Garmin Venu 4 as the only pick on ChatGPT's list that works on both platforms, with the reply-to-text caveat for iPhone users.

angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the maker's solar panel stops charging the battery below 32°F (0°C). Both feeders still run below freezing, Birdfy to 14°F and Kiwibit to −4°F, so through a freezing spell the battery only drains and is not refilled, however sunny it is.

It still works, but you have to charge it indoors by hand. So in cold climates battery size matters more than panel wattage. My own reasoning, which no source states: Birdfy's 9,000 mAh feeders (Feeder 2 series, Feeder Metal 2 4K) should outlast the 5,000 mAh Soliom BF08 and Bird Buddy's 3,800–3,900 mAh units on a cold, non-charging stretch. pages.why_used: The cited Newport FAQ and Minn Kota pages say only that the Newport's meter misreads lithium. None quotes Newport's own store line that the Smart Battery Box is 'not compatible with lithium batteries'. None says that the lithium-rated LiTime box's only breaker is 16 A, or that its 8.66 in interior is too short for 9.38–9.45 in tall Group 31 batteries. pages.why_used: None of the cited guides gives the built-in preamp's actual line-output voltage for any deck. One of them says outright that no output is stated for any pick. Angle A puts maker figures on five decks: AT-LP70X 252 mV, AT-LP120XUSB 240 mV, Sony PS-LX3BT 180 mV and the Fluance RT81 and RT81+ at 140 mV each. That shows the AT-LP70X is about 5 dB hotter into powered speakers, and that the RT81+ upgrade adds no line level. Angle C's Sony finding goes in as a supporting detail. None of the site's products is a turntable, and Amazon blocked the ASIN lookup, so the pick (Audio-Technica AT-LP70X) is a product we don't list and its link goes to the maker's page.

Fluance rates both the RT81 and the RT81+ at 140 mV (−17 dBV) with no test condition. That is about 5 dB less signal into the same powered speakers, from a preamp with about 4–5 dB less implied gain (32 dB and 31 dB, against A-T's stated 36 dB).
angles.decides: This supports ChatGPT's pick of the AT-LP70X for a shopper who will plug straight into powered speakers. Its line out is about 1.8× the voltage of the RT81 and RT81+ (20·log10(252/140) ≈ 5.1 dB). All of them sit below the −10 dBV (316 mV) consumer line reference, and the Fluance pair sits furthest below it. The Fluance therefore needs more volume from the speakers or amp to play as loud. The RT81+'s stronger cartridge (4.0 mV against 3.5 mV) does not raise its stated line output, which stays at 140 mV. As a result, upgrading from the RT81 to the RT81+ gives no extra level at the LINE output, going by Fluance's own figures.

Epoch is the premium pick for high-draw or cold-weather installs, and a single LiTime or Redodo fits loads up to about 2,000 W unless you add a second battery in parallel. On cycle life, Epoch's 3,500+ looks lower than LiTime's 4,000+ at 100% depth of discharge. For a shopper who just needs a 24V battery with no inverter link, this confirms that the cheaper LiTime and Redodo Bluetooth models are enough. The Epoch premium pick offers only Bluetooth, so it cannot join a closed loop either. Battle Born is on Victron's list, but only as a drop-in with 'no integration or communication, such CANbus', so being listed is not the same as closed-loop support.

pages.why_used: The guide ChatGPT cited (extruly) blames fused print-in-place joints on first-layer squish but never names the setting. The top-ranked guide (3dprintgearlab) recommends −0.15 to −0.2 mm of first-layer shrink but never says the A1 mini ships at 0 mm. This page reads each maker's stock slicer profile: Bambu A1 mini 0 mm, A1 0.075 mm, QIDI and Flashforge 0.15 mm. It turns that into one setting to change, and gives a named measured result (IgorsLab: gaps down to 0.15 mm turned on the A1 mini).

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got puts the A1 mini's two headline numbers, 500 mm/s top speed and 'sub 48 dB' noise, on the same basis. Owners describe the quiet figure as a silent-mode result: silent mode runs at about 50% speed, and the part-cooling fan at 100% is said to go above 48 dB. Bambu's own spec page could not be opened to confirm the condition.
angles.decides: It confirms the A1 mini rather than changing the pick. For fidget toys the slower, quieter mode costs little. extruly already advises dropping outer walls to 150 mm/s for clean print-in-place joints, which is well below the 500 mm/s headline. So the speed spec should not decide between the A1 mini and the A1. Build size (180 vs 256 mm) and the AMS lite colour option decide it. The page can say plainly that the quiet figure and the fast figure are not reached at the same time.

The A1 mini's 180 mm bed has a 254.6 mm diagonal, so a 200 mm articulated dragon fits only if it is laid diagonally and is no wider than 54.6 mm. The A1's 256 mm bed holds it straight and has a 362.0 mm diagonal.
angles.decides: This confirms ChatGPT's A1 mini pick for typical fidgets: spinners, gear rings and 120 mm dragons fit straight on its 180 mm bed. It also sets a hard switch point. Any print-in-place piece longer than 180 mm has to go diagonally on the mini, and the length plus width must stay at or under 254.6 mm. A long snake or a wide-winged 200 mm dragon will not fit, so those buyers need the A1 (256 mm straight, 362 mm diagonal). The A1 also has 2.02× the bed area, roughly twice the fidgets per batch, which matters for selling.

angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that Bambu's own stock slicer profiles for the A1 mini apply no elephant-foot compensation ("elefant_foot_compensation": "0"). Done that way, Tenergy's 10,000 mAh D page makes no self-discharge claim at all, so it is not shown to be a low-self-discharge cell. It weakens ChatGPT's 'Tenergy Premium 10,000 mAh for frequent use' pick for anyone who stores cells, because Tenergy states no retention for it. It also undercuts EBL's 1,200-cycle 'value' case, since EBL itself also says 500 for D cells. For storage, the rated mAh matters less than whether the maker states a retention figure.

From the makers' own US store prices and cell weights: Tenergy Premium D 10,000 mAh costs $0.77 per rated Wh at 33.6 Wh/lb. Tenergy Centura 8,000 mAh, ChatGPT's 'best overall', costs $0.91/Wh at 30.0 Wh/lb. Powerex costs $1.66 per guaranteed Wh at Maha's list price. A BudgetLightForum tester measured EBL D cells at 6,500–7,000 mAh, which would push EBL's 4-pack to $1.19–1.28/Wh.
angles.decides: It changes the value pick. Per rated Wh at the maker's own store, Tenergy Premium D 10,000 mAh ($36.99 for 4, $0.77/Wh) beats Centura ($0.91/Wh). It also beats EBL's retail 4-pack ($0.83/Wh). EBL's separate 'D2' 4-count at $28.88 works out to $0.60/Wh on paper. But EBL's 126 g cell weight and a named forum test (6,500–7,000 mAh) suggest its 10,000 mAh rating is inflated, so its real cost is about $1.19–1.28/Wh. Centura stays the storage pick because of its retention claim, but it costs 18% more per Wh than Tenergy Premium. Powerex is the only candidate with a published guaranteed minimum (9,000 mAh), and at $1.66 per guaranteed Wh it is the premium choice, not a value one.

pages.why_used: The cited pages (FDA safety notice, Samsung's US launch release, Hilo's comparison blog, Android Authority, Cardilog, Wareable and TechRadar on the Watch D3) never put the candidates on one accuracy yardstick. None states that the Watch D2 passed ISO 81060-2 while the Watch D3 being recommended has not been validated and was measured outside the 5 mmHg mean bound. None says the validated Omron HeartGuide code is discontinued while the BP8000-M still sold carries an unvalidated code.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that on a single accuracy yardstick (passing the ISO 81060-2 clinical validation) only the Huawei Watch D2 among the cards passes for the general population, while the newer Watch D3 it recommended has not been validated yet (Fnac measured it 7/6 mmHg below an Omron cuff), and the 'FDA-cleared' Omron HeartGuide is discontinued and has a second model code (HEM-6411T-ZM) with no published validation.
angles.decides: It moves the cuff pick from the Watch D3 to the Watch D2. The D2 is the only cuff watch on offer with a pass under ISO 81060-2 (85-subject primary study plus stress and ambulatory studies). The D3 has no validation yet, and a named reviewer measured it outside the 5 mmHg mean-error bound. It also takes the Omron HeartGuide out of the 'medical-focused' slot: Medaval lists it as discontinued, and the clearance (K182481) covers the HEM-6410T-ZM, so the HEM-6411T-ZM code is not a validated buy. Samsung, Hilo Core and Apple stay as trend or notification tools. Samsung and Hilo call their products wellness features, and neither publishes a validation result for its estimates.

angles.name: Derive
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states how many blood pressure readings each device gets per charge. From the makers' battery test conditions: Huawei Watch D2 and D3 get about 36 cuff readings per charge at 6 a day for 6 days, and up to 96 when 24-hour ABPM (ambulatory blood pressure monitoring) is on at 15-minute intervals, though then the battery lasts only 1 day. Omron HeartGuide gets about 16 cuff readings per charge at 8 a day for 2 days. Hilo Core gets up to 210–525 optical estimates, and none of those are cuff readings.
angles.decides: This confirms the Huawei Watch D2/D3 as the pick for someone who wants many real cuff readings and still a weeklong battery: about 36 cuff readings per charge, against about 16 for the Omron HeartGuide, which also has to be charged about every 2 days. It also exposes a catch the answers miss. A full 24-hour ABPM session runs the Huawei battery down to about 1 day, and Expert Reviews' Jonathan Bray saw about 3 days when testing 'multiple times per day'. Hilo Core gives far more readings per charge, but they are optical estimates checked against a cuff, not cuff readings. The figure helps choose a watch but does not overturn the medical caveat.

angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that Huawei's own compatibility table for the Watch D2 marks cuff blood-pressure measurement and 24-hour ambulatory BP (ABPM) as supported on iPhone (iOS 13.0+), the same as on Android, and that both airbag strap sizes come in the box: M for 130–160 mm wrists, L for 161–210 mm. For comparison, Samsung's BP needs a Galaxy phone, and Apple's hypertension notifications show no readings and leave out Apple Watch SE.
angles.decides: ChatGPT ended by asking 'Which phone do you use?', and this finding answers that. For iPhone users who want real mmHg readings, the Huawei Watch D2/D3 is the only cuff watch here whose maker lists BP and 24-hour BP as working on iOS. It is still an import with no FDA clearance and no US warranty. Apple Watch gives only hypertension alerts, on Series 9+/Ultra 2+ and not SE, so Dealectric's listed Apple Watch SE 3 gets no BP feature at all. Galaxy Watch BP works only with a Galaxy phone, and only on a watch and phone bought in the US. Dealectric's listed Galaxy Watch 8 qualifies under that rule. Android users on non-Samsung phones get Huawei Health from AppGallery, not Google Play. Hilo Core needs iOS 16+ or Android 14+.
products: Samsung Galaxy Watch (Watch4 and later, incl. Watch8/Watch9)

angles.name: Mechanism
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the Huawei Watch D2's cuff is an inflating airbag that only works when the watch is held level with the heart on a wrist 130–210 mm around, using whichever of the two included straps fits (M 130–160 mm, L 161–210 mm), and that Huawei itself warns that arrhythmia, a heart rate below 40 or above 180 bpm, or severe arteriosclerosis can make readings fail or come out wrong.
angles.decides: This confirms that the cuff watch is the only kind in ChatGPT's picks that actually measures blood pressure rather than estimating it. It also adds conditions that ChatGPT left out. A shopper whose wrist is outside 130–210 mm, or who has atrial fibrillation or frequent premature beats, should not count on the D2's cuff and should use an upper-arm cuff instead. Turning on the D2's 24-hour monitoring cuts battery life to about 1 day. On the Samsung side, the feature needs a Galaxy phone on Android 12 or later and a separately bought upper-arm cuff every 28 days. Samsung also says its Health Monitor app works only on devices bought in a country where the service is offered.

angles.name: Named measurements
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that in the5krunner's four-person seated test against an Omron upper-arm cuff, the Huawei Watch D3 read low on 18 of 20 systolic readings and 16 of 20 diastolic readings. The per-person average gaps reached -14/-8 mmHg (139/90 on the cuff, 125/82 on the watch) and -13/-17 mmHg (115/76 on the cuff, 102/59 on the watch). Notebookcheck's three-reading test found the D3's mean systolic reading only 0.5% below an Omron RS4 wrist monitor's, but its diastolic reading about 11% higher.
angles.decides: ChatGPT's second chat ranks the Huawei Watch D3 'Best for actual blood pressure measurements'. Named measurements partly support this: on systolic, Notebookcheck measured the D3's mean 0.5% below an Omron RS4. They also qualify it: the5krunner found the D3 read low on most readings across four people, with two people reading 13–17 mmHg low on one number. Only the Omron HeartGuide (HEM-6410T-ZM) has a published ISO 81060-2 validation with numbers: -0.9 ± 7.6 / -1.1 ± 6.1 mmHg (Kuwabara et al., 2019). For a shopper who wants readings they can act on, this favors the HeartGuide, or at least checking any cuff watch against an upper-arm cuff. The cuffless options are a different case. Notebookcheck's single pair for the Hilo Band was 5/8 mmHg high, and a 2026 Digital Health study found smartwatch errors grew to 3.4/5.1 mmHg once blood pressure moved 10 mmHg from the calibration point. Both point to using these bands for trends, not for spot readings.

pages.why_used: The cited rival pages (3dtoolchangers.com/printers, 3dprinteray.com/toolchanger-printers) give only maker swap-time claims and prices. None has a named tester's results on the same model. This page has them: CNC Kitchen's 4-colour cube took under 4 h on the U1 and Prusa XL and about 7 h on the Bambu H2C, and a colour change took about 40 s on the H2C against 10–15 s on a toolchanger. It also has Notebookcheck's Creator 5 Pro waste and prep-time figures and today's prices: U1 $699, Creator 5 Pro $849. The pick, the Snapmaker U1, is not a product we list. Snapmaker isn't in our programs and amzcheck found no U1 on Amazon. Our QIDI and Flashforge Adventurer 5M Pro printers have a single nozzle and win no segment of this question, so the page adds no product of ours.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the U1's 5-second swap and the INDX's 12-second swap are measured differently. Prusa's ~12 s runs from the last extrusion on one tool to the first extrusion on the next, while Snapmaker's 5 s is an undefined 'typical' lab result. A hands-on reviewer timed the U1 at 10–12 s per colour change, which is about the same as the INDX, not 2.4× faster.
angles.decides: It removes the U1's apparent speed edge over the INDX. Measured the same way, both swap in about 10–12 s, so the $749-vs-$1,999 choice comes down to enclosure and chamber heat (INDX up to 55 °C, U1 only an optional unheated Top Cover), waste per swap (INDX 0.013 g claimed with no prime tower, U1 about 0.049 g measured from its prime tower), and the INDX's smaller Y travel. Swap speed doesn't separate them. This confirms the U1 as the value pick but not as a faster one.

angles.name: Derive
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states how much tool-change time and waste a full job adds. Per 1,000 tool changes, the Prusa CORE One+ INDX spends about 3.3 h swapping (12 s each) and wastes about 13 g of filament (0.013 g each). The Snapmaker U1 spends about 1.4 h (5 s each). So on a print with many colour changes, the INDX's low-waste nozzle swap adds about 1.9 h per 1,000 changes.
angles.decides: For dense multicolour work (thousands of changes per plate), this favours the U1 or Creator 5 Pro on time, since a full toolhead swaps in about 5 s. The INDX makes sense when the buyer cares more about nozzle or material variety and near-zero waste (13 g per 1,000 changes) than about speed. Its 8-tool configuration also brings the price per tool close to the budget machines: $281 assembled, $244 as a kit.

pages.why_used: The two cited TP-Link FAQs (947 and 83) explain how to set up schedules and Auto-Off. Neither says what happens when the internet or power goes out. TP-Link's own FAQ 2463 does: schedules, timers and Away Mode run on the plug with the internet down, there is a 32-rule cap per plug, the timers stop after a power cut until the plug goes back online to reset its clock, the priority order is Timer > Schedule > Away, and Tapo's Away Mode can run past midnight while Kasa's can't. The product pages add the 1/6 HP motor limit behind the '15 A' rating, against 1/2 HP on the EP40. Angle A is the only one that is fully sourced from the maker for every row, and it changes the pick for outdoor/motor loads and for cabins with no internet.

angles.decides: This confirms Kasa or Tapo for the usual lamp-or-fan schedule: the schedules are stored on the plug and run with the internet down. It changes the pick in two cases. (1) If the timer must recover by itself after a power cut while the internet is also out, as in a cabin, a holiday house or an aquarium during a storm, these plugs stop running schedules until they're back online. That points to the plain programmable timer ChatGPT offered as its 'No Wi-Fi required' option. pages.why_used: Both of ChatGPT's searches ended in 'solar panel compatibility', and its answer told shoppers to 'choose a panel explicitly compatible with your exact model' without naming any. The cited rivals (SafeWise, Bob Vila, HomeGearLab, RottenWiFi) give no panel model numbers or generation exclusions, apart from HomeGearLab's one Blink line and its mention of USB-C for Ring. This page adds a maker-sourced fit chart (Reolink, eufy, Ring, Arlo VMA by camera model number, Blink), each maker's exclusions, Reolink's 0 °C charging floor and its 9 m extension limit.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got turns the makers' sunlight claims into one comparable figure. eufy's '2 hours of sun' for the SoloCam S340 rests on a harvest of 800–1,200 mAh a day against 100–200 mAh of use, so it carries a 4–12× margin. Reolink's '20 minutes with the 3 W panel' (Argus PT Ultra) works out to only about 1 Wh at the panel's rated output, and Tapo's '50 minutes' (C465) is measured at lab standard sun of 1,000 W/m² with up to 100 events a day. The gap between 2 hours and 20 minutes comes from how each maker builds its claim, not from a 6× difference in panels. pages.why_used: The rival pages give Synology's 'more than 2 GB' VM rule and Home Assistant's 2 GB VM minimum separately. None of them subtracts the HAOS VM from each NAS's shipped RAM. This page does: 6 GB left on the DXP2800, TS-264 and DXP4800 Plus, 2 GB on the DS925+, and none on a stock DS225+, which cannot start a VM at all.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got puts these together: a stock Synology DS225+ ships with exactly 2 GB, Synology's VMM rule says VMs run only on a NAS with more than 2 GB, and Home Assistant says an HAOS VM needs at least 2 GB. So the DS225+ cannot run an HAOS VM until a RAM module is added, even though its spec sheet lists '2 recommended VM instances'. On a 2 GB DS220+, VMM offered the auto-generated VM only 272 MB.
angles.decides: It rules out a stock DS225+ for an HAOS VM, so 'DS225+ / DS925+' on our page should become 'DS925+, or a DS225+ only with an added 4 GB module'. The DS925+ (4 GB ECC, 8 recommended VM instances) and the QNAP TS-264 (8 GB, where Virtualization Station needs at least 4 GB and QNAP advises giving VMs at most 50% of memory, leaving about 4 GB for HAOS) both clear the 2 GB HAOS minimum out of the box. On USB, all three main makers pass through a single device rather than a whole port or controller, so USB support doesn't separate them. On QNAP the only USB-speed caveat is guest-OS USB 3 support, which HAOS's Linux kernel meets, and the TS-264 also has USB 2.0 ports. UGREEN's DH2300 and DH4300 Plus cannot run VMs at all, so only the DXP models qualify.

angles.name: Mechanism
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states the mechanism that decides whether a passed-through Zigbee stick keeps working. The KVM/libvirt layer gives a USB device a device number at connect time, and only the physical port number stays the same (libvirt's own words). When a stick resets or re-enumerates, the VM keeps waiting for the old number. Sticks also differ: a ConBee II (CDC-ACM, /dev/ttyACM) failed on a UGREEN VM where a Sonoff ZBDongle-E, which uses a WCH CH34x-family serial bridge, worked straight away. The Home Assistant ZBT-2 disappears from Synology VMM during its mandatory first firmware flash.
angles.decides: The finding moves the deciding factor from NAS brand to stick. All three NAS VM apps can pass a USB device through. Whether it survives a reboot, replug or firmware flash depends on how the hypervisor rebinds it and on the stick's USB-serial bridge. For the pick: on UGREEN, Synology or QNAP, use a stick that has been reported working under VM passthrough (Sonoff ZBDongle-E on UGREEN). Avoid the ConBee II. If buying a ZBT-2, flash its firmware on another computer before passing it through. Expect to restart the VM, not just HAOS, after the stick drops. This supports ChatGPT's network-coordinator fallback (SMLIGHT SLZB-06), which avoids USB re-enumeration entirely, and makes it stronger.

angles.decides: This doesn't decide whether USB Zigbee passthrough works. It does work as a tiebreak on running cost for a box that's on 24/7. ChatGPT's top pick, the QNAP TS-264, drew 26.5 W idle in PCWorld's test, against 18.6 W for the DXP2800 and DS224+ in ComputerBase's test. That gap is about 69 kWh a year: 7.9 W × 8,760 h. pages.why_used: I could read one of the cited pages in full (StackandValue) and the start of a second (Dupple). Neither says what Windows does to a Bluetooth speaker that supports hands-free calling. TechRadar, Tom's Hardware, Tom's Guide and PC Gamer returned only their titles, and Wired blocked the fetch, so the angle agents could not rule them out. Microsoft's driver docs say that once any app opens the speaker's mic, playback switches to mono at 8 or 16 kHz, and on Windows 10 the stereo stream is thrown away. This page gives each candidate's Bluetooth profile or mic listing and its wired fallback, and picks the A2DP-only Creative Pebble Pro, which plays USB audio.

A PC user who wants full power is therefore on Bluetooth (SBC only) or AUX. On a PC's own USB-C port with USB audio they get 10 W RMS (Pebble Pro) or 15 W RMS (Pebble X Plus). The mains-powered Creative T60 gives 30 W RMS while taking USB-C audio.
angles.decides: It changes the pick for a shopper who wants wired USB audio from a PC, which is the setup both ChatGPT answers pushed for gaming and calls. In that setup the Pebble Pro ($66.49) gives 10 W RMS and the Pebble X Plus ($123.49) gives 15 W RMS. The T60 ($94.99, with its own 18 V 2 A adapter) gives 30 W RMS while playing USB-C audio. ChatGPT's 'best overall value' Pebble Pro is a third as loud as the T60 in the mode ChatGPT recommended, unless the shopper buys a 30 W PD brick and moves to Bluetooth SBC or AUX. The Pebble Pro is still the right pick for a small desk where 10 W RMS is enough. For more volume over USB, the T60 is the better buy, and it costs less than the X Plus.

A Pebble Pro or Pebble X Plus buyer who adds the 30 W PD adapter for full power still needs a second connection for sound: USB-C to the PC, Bluetooth, or AUX. The Pebble V3 must stay USB-powered even in Bluetooth mode. The Pebble Pro stays the value pick for a PC with a USB-C port, since Creative rates 10 W RMS from a 10 W USB-C port. The T60 and M60 have no such power-source caveat on the pages I read, and the T60 ships with its own 18 V 2 A AC adapter.

angles.name: Mechanism
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that Windows switches a Bluetooth speaker that supports the Hands-Free Profile to mono playback at 8 kHz or 16 kHz as soon as any app opens that speaker's microphone input. Microsoft says this happens on Windows 11 and that Windows 10 discards the stereo stream outright. Microsoft also lists only SBC, AAC, aptX Classic and aptX Adaptive (aptX Adaptive only on select Qualcomm radios) as Windows A2DP codecs, so a mic-less, A2DP-only speaker such as the Creative Pebble Pro, or a wired USB-C connection, avoids the problem.
angles.decides: For a PC used for both media and calls, pick a speaker that is A2DP-only with no built-in mic, or one with a wired USB-C audio input. That confirms the Creative Pebble Pro (A2DP only, SBC, USB audio, no built-in mic) as the safe default. A single portable speaker with a hands-free mic, such as the Marshall Emberton III, is a poor PC choice when calls matter. The moment Teams or Discord opens its mic, Windows drops the speaker to mono 8 kHz or 16 kHz, and the Emberton III has no wired audio input to fall back on (its USB-C is listed only for charging). The Creative T60 lists HFP alongside A2DP, so Windows 11 creates a mic input for it. Over Bluetooth, keep the PC's default mic set to something else, or use the T60's USB-C audio. A further point for the Pebble Pro: the 30 W RMS figure needs a separate 30 W USB PD adapter, which is not included. Powered from a PC port it is 10 W RMS.

None of them gives a measured delay for any recommended bar, converts it to film frames or checks it against the ITU lip-sync limit. None notes that the portable Bose Flex (2nd Gen) has no wired input. This page gives the HT-S100F's measured 62 ms (ARC) and 70 ms (optical), which is 1.5–1.7 frames and inside the ITU's 125 ms limit. It also sets out a wired-input check for every candidate.

Both use SBC-only Bluetooth receivers, and the Samsung B630F's 'Bluetooth TV Connection' works only with Samsung TVs. For a lag-free TV link, use the HDMI ARC or optical input, which every candidate has. Don't count on Bluetooth from the TV.
