pages.why_used: Every page ChatGPT cited compares the Yamaha CD-S303, Onkyo C-7030 and Denon DCD-600NE on the makers' own 105 / 107 / 112 dB claims; none carries a bench measurement. This page adds Audio Science Review's and Hi-Fi News' lab figures, which put the Yamaha and Denon at the same 95 dB noise floor and give the output-level gap, so the choice falls to outputs and USB, where the Yamaha wins.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got puts the three makers' noise, distortion and output figures on one line and says that the Yamaha CD-S303's Pure Direct mode switches off the optical and coaxial outputs that are its main hardware edge over the optical-only Denon DCD-600NE, nor that Denon's own manual (12 W, 4.3 kg) and US product page (13 W, 4.0 kg) disagree with each other.
angles.decides: On the makers' own numbers the Denon leads on S/N (112 dB) and dynamic range (101 dB) but has no coaxial output; the Onkyo is the only one with a headphone jack and is the cheapest; the Yamaha is the only one with USB playback but loses both digital outputs whenever Pure Direct is on. For a shopper feeding an external DAC the Yamaha's advantage is conditional, which confirms the Onkyo as the practical pick and the Denon as the analog-only pick.

angles.name: Derive
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that a Denon DCD-600NE left powered but idle draws 12 W against 0.3 W in standby, that its 30-minute Auto Standby ships switched off, or that the Yamaha-vs-Denon running-cost gap works out to about 1.5 kWh a year at 2 h of play a day.
angles.decides: Running cost cannot separate the Yamaha CD-S303 and Denon DCD-600NE: 11 W vs 12 W playing and 0.2 W vs 0.3 W in standby is about 1.5 kWh a year apart at 2 h/day. What does matter is behaviour: the Denon ships with Auto Standby off, so a forgotten unit burns 12 W around the clock (about 105 kWh/yr) until the owner holds POWER 5 s to enable the 30-minute timer. Both put out 2.0 V RMS on RCA, so neither needs a different amp input gain; the FiiO DM13 line out is 2.5 V RMS, about 1.9 dB hotter, which matters if the shopper is weighing the portable FiiO against a full-width deck for the same stereo.

angles.name: Compatibility
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the Onkyo C-7030's one-remote/auto-input RI link works only with Onkyo RI-equipped amplifiers and still needs an analog RCA connection even when you use the digital output, or that the Denon DCD-600NE's rear IR CONTROL jacks are for Denon network audio players, not an amplifier link.
angles.decides: Confirms the Onkyo C-7030 only as the pick for a shopper who owns an Onkyo RI amp or receiver (one remote, auto input switch); for any other brand of stereo amp the RI jack is dead weight and the Onkyo should be connected only by RCA/optical/coaxial. The Denon DCD-600NE has no amplifier link jack and no coaxial output, so it suits an amp with an optical input or RCA only. Yamaha CD-S303 remains the pick for USB/FLAC playback (rival-stated), but maker confirmation of its USB limits was not reachable.

angles.name: Mechanism
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the Denon DCD-600NE and Onkyo C-7030 both put out a fixed 2.0 V RMS analog line level (Onkyo rated into 600 Ω), so the stereo must offer a line-level CD/AUX/TAPE input and the player cannot drive volume itself, nor that the Denon caps data discs at 512 files/256 folders, 48–320 kbps MP3/WMA, refuses non-finalized CD-Rs and copy-protected WMA, and outputs digital on optical only.
angles.decides: For a stereo with a spare analog CD/AUX/TAPE input the mechanism does not separate the three: each delivers a fixed ~2.0 V RMS line level over RCA, so any of them works and the player has no volume control of its own (a PHONO input is the wrong place). The mechanism only decides the pick when the stereo's free input is digital: a coaxial-only input rules out the Denon DCD-600NE (optical only); any digital link needs Pure Direct off on the Yamaha CD-S303 or Mode 1 on the Denon, else silence. For shoppers with burned discs, the Denon manual says non-finalized CD-Rs and copy-protected WMA will not play and caps a data disc at 512 files and 320 kbps.

angles.name: Named measurements
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states an independently measured noise, distortion or jitter figure for any candidate: Hi-Fi News measured the Denon DCD-600 at 95.3 dB A-weighted S/N, 0.0013% THD and 480 psec jitter, and an Audio Science Review member measured the Yamaha CD-S303 at 95.7 dB dynamic range, 0.0022% THD+N and 1.74 V output.
angles.decides: It confirms rather than overturns the pick: both of the two most-cited budget players measure to roughly the same 95 dB noise floor, well below the makers' 105 dB (Yamaha) and 110 dB (Denon) claims, so neither has a measurable sound-quality edge and the choice can rest on price, outputs and features. Two usable details: the Denon's 1.92 Vrms output is near the 2 V standard while the Yamaha's 1.74 Vrms sits 1.2 dB low (the Yamaha will sound quieter at the same volume setting), and the Yamaha was verified bit-perfect as a transport over optical, which matters for anyone feeding an external DAC. No independent measurement exists for the Onkyo C-7030, so its 107 dB claim stays unverified.

The NAD C 538 ties on outputs at the same street price but has no USB. If the shopper's amp has only an optical input or they want a headphone jack, the $139.99 Fosi Audio Merak or $164.99 FiiO DM13 become the budget alternative; the Marantz CD60 at $1,100 is the step up with 118 dB S/N and a headphone jack.

None of them explains that AM comes in through an antenna inside the case and that you aim it by turning the whole unit. This page sorts every candidate by the bands listed in its maker spec or manual, adds today's prices and says which models skip AM.

That puts its real total at about 2.2 W, against the '3 W' or '20 W' figures rival lists put beside it. The 20 W Panasonic SC-PM270 is also the only one of these that is AC-only and FM-only, with no AM band.

That leaves the battery boomboxes with AM, the Sony CFD-S70 (6 C cells, AM 530–1,710 kHz) and the Jensen CD-560 (8 C cells). Their headline watts are not comparable: Sony's honest US figure is 1.1 W/ch, and Jensen publishes no measured rating on a maker page. So pick on battery count and band coverage, not on watts. The battery-life claims are also on different bases. Sony states about 10 h of CD play at volume 23 on Sony alkaline cells. Jensen's '50 hours' comes from a brand rep's Target Q&A answer, with no mode or volume given.

pages.why_used: The cited rivals (OutdoorGearLab, plus GearJunkie's one BougeRV CRD45 bundle) list which cords each cooler ships with. None of them says which maker battery fits which cooler: BougeRV's 240 Wh internal battery fits neither the 23 qt nor the CRPRO30, ICECO's bank is external on the VL45, and Dometic's PLB40 costs $539.99. None of them adds up cooler plus battery for each pick, so a shopper who answers 'need a built-in battery' gets no priced path.

angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the US Dometic CFX5 45 (R1234yf, SKU 97000050755) is rated at 1.05 Ah/h (about 302 Wh/day at 90°F ambient, 39°F inside), 38% more than the 0.76 Ah/h Dometic gives for the AU/NZ R600a version. They also don't say that the other makers state power on bases you can't compare: Anker gives runtime at 77°F with an empty cooler in Eco mode, and ICECO gives kWh per 24 h with no ambient temperature.

Converted to Wh/day, the US CFX5 45's own rating is about 302 Wh/day at 90°F, so a 500 Wh station covers about 1.7 days before DC-conversion losses. Anker's claim works out to about 134 Wh/day, but that is at 77°F, so it doesn't mean the Anker is more than twice as efficient. On the one common basis we have (OGL's 75°F lab), the measured gap is small: 5.8 W vs 6.8 W. In the table, the footnote is the finding: makers quote power at 77°F, at 90°F and at no stated temperature, and the US and AU versions of the same Dometic carry different ratings.

angles.name: Derive
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got gives a hot-weather daily energy figure or days on a power station. Dometic's own spec for the US CFX5 45 is 1.05 Ah/h at 32 °C (90 °F) outside and 4 °C (39 °F) inside. That works out to about 302 Wh a day, so a 1,024 Wh station (EcoFlow DELTA 3, Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2) lasts about 3.4 days in summer heat. OutdoorGearLab's 75 °F lab draw of 6.8 W gives about 6.3 days, so heat almost doubles the draw.
angles.decides: It doesn't change which cooler to pick. It changes what to pair with it. For summer car camping, size the station at about 300 Wh per day for a 45 L compressor cooler, not the 160–200 Wh/day the 75 °F lab numbers suggest. A weekend in the heat needs about 600 Wh, which rules out 245–300 Wh stations (RIVER 3, Tenergy T320, ALLPOWERS R600) for anything past one night. The 1,024 Wh class is the right pairing for a 3-day trip. ChatGPT's '500 Wh ≈ 1–2 days' holds in heat (500/302 = 1.7 days) but undersells mild weather (500/163 = 3.1 days).

On the CRPRO30 the battery path is an external 266 Wh power station sold as a kit for $389.99. For a shopper who picks the battery option, the BougeRV pick should be the CRX3 23QT ($199.99) or CRX3 30QT ($249.99), which take the internal 240 Wh battery. For the 45 L tier, ICECO's VL45 has no internal battery. ICECO sells it with a separate 250 Wh 'Magnetic Power Bank' ($663.10 bundle), and only the VL45PLUS ($799) is listed as 'Magnetic Battery Ready'. Dometic's battery for the CFX5 45 is the external PLB40 at $539.99, which almost doubles the cost of the $997 fridge. Of the four, only Dealectric's own Anker SOLIX EverFrost 2 40L has a removable battery included.

Without that setting, the plan of running the fridge off the car overnight is the one that strands the shopper.

What it changes is the advice that goes with it: the shopper can run the BougeRV, ICECO VL45 or Dometic CFX5 straight off the car, as long as the battery protection is set to HIGH. A built-in-battery model (Anker SOLIX EverFrost 2) or a power station (Dealectric lists several) is what makes overnight off-grid use work without touching the starter battery. pages.why_used: The cited rivals (firstlayerlab, 3dprintgearlab) list the P2S chamber only as 'passive' or 'no active heating listed' and give the Q2's 65 °C without its heater wattage. None of them places the P2S's 50 °C passive ceiling and CNC Kitchen's measured 50.3–54.1 °C next to the Q2's separate 280 W heater, and none shows that the $349 Q2C drops that heater for $100 less on the same frame. This page covers all three.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the Bambu Lab P2S's own '50 °C chamber' figure is a passive limit with no heater: it comes from bed heat held in by an automatic air flap, and owners log about 37–52 °C depending on the aux-fan setting. The QIDI Q2's '65 °C' is a setpoint held by a dedicated 280 W chamber heater. The two figures look comparable but are not.
angles.decides: This supports ChatGPT's split pick. For PLA and PETG, the P2S's passive chamber is enough. For ABS, ASA and nylon, the Q2 at the same $449 has a 280 W heater that holds 65 °C. The P2S's 50 °C is a best case that one owner logged at 37–42 °C with the right aux fan at 100% in heating mode. It also warns shoppers off the QIDI Q2C ($349): it has the same 270 × 270 × 256 mm build volume, but its US store blurb doesn't list chamber heating, while the Q2's blurb does.

angles.name: Derive
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got works out the cost of a heated chamber in dollars per liter of build space. On QIDI's own US store, the QIDI Q2 costs $449 for 18.66 L ($24.06 per liter). The QIDI Q2C has the same 270 × 270 × 256 mm volume for $349 ($18.70 per liter), and its listing does not mention the Q2's 65 °C active chamber heating. On QIDI's own figures, the heated chamber costs $100. The Q2's 280 W heater can use up to 2.8 kWh over a 10-hour ABS print, on top of the printer's 350 W rating.
angles.decides: This supports ChatGPT's split: the QIDI Q2 for ABS, ASA and nylon, where an actively heated chamber matters, and a cheaper passive printer otherwise. It also adds an option ChatGPT never mentioned. A shopper printing only PLA or PETG can buy the QIDI Q2C for $349, the same build volume as the Q2 for $100 less ($18.70 vs $24.06 per liter). The extra $100 for the Q2 only pays off for engineering filaments. Dealectric already lists the qidi-q2 (awin:qidi), so a Q2 vs Q2C section would point to a product we can link.

angles.name: Compatibility
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the add-on multicolor units for two of its recommended enclosed printers are tied to specific models: the QIDI Box comes in separate Plus4, Q2 and Max4 versions (different Box Hub and signal cable, $40.99 kit to move it to another printer), and Creality's K1-series CFS upgrade kit for the K1C works only with the integrated-nozzle hotend and keeps the top cover from closing fully, so the K1C stops being fully enclosed for ABS unless you print the height-extension part.
angles.decides: This backs the QIDI Q2 as the pick for a shopper who wants an enclosed printer for ABS/ASA now and multicolor later. QIDI's US Q2 page says it works with the QIDI Box, and QIDI says the Box can dry and print at the same time (up to 65 °C) and chain up to 4 units. Buy the Q2 version of the Box, or plan $40.99 for the upgrade kit if you move it to another printer. It counts against the Creality K1C for the same shopper. ChatGPT pitched it as 'enclosed', but adding Creality's CFS means an integrated-nozzle hotend, a top cover that no longer closes fully (Creality supplies height-extension files for ABS), and a smaller 220 × 215 × 250 mm print volume. The finding doesn't change the pick for a shopper printing PLA/PETG in one color.

angles.name: Mechanism
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got gives the P2S's chamber ceiling. It has no chamber heater: its only heat is the bed, held in by a motorized airflow flap that switches to recirculation, which tops out at about 50 °C. The QIDI Q2 adds a separate 280 W PTC chamber heater (rated 350 W + 280 W) that holds up to 65 °C whatever the bed is doing.
angles.decides: This backs ChatGPT's split. If the shopper mostly prints PLA, PETG or small ABS/ASA parts, the P2S works: its bed heat, held in by the flap, reaches about 50 °C, and in cooling mode it pulls in outside air so PLA can print with the door shut. If they print large ABS/ASA parts, PC or nylon, they need a heater that works independently of the bed, and among the cards shown only the QIDI Q2 has one (65 °C, 280 W PTC). The P1S, K1C and Adventurer 5M Pro all rely on bed heat alone. The Q2 heater pushes the rated draw to 630 W, which does not affect a standard 15 A US outlet. For a PLA-only buyer the Q2's heater is no advantage. QIDI's own blog lists heat creep among the risks of too much chamber heat.

angles.name: Named measurements
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states a measured chamber temperature for any of these printers. CNC Kitchen's thermocouples read 50.3 °C and 54.1 °C inside the Bambu Lab P2S's passive chamber, with the bed at 100–110 °C. Clever Creations timed the Creality K1C's chamber at 30 minutes to rise from 25 °C to its 38 °C maximum.
angles.decides: The measurements back ChatGPT's split pick and make it more precise. The P2S's passive chamber was measured at about 50–54 °C, which is far warmer than the K1C's measured 38 °C maximum. That makes the P2S a fair choice for occasional ABS/ASA. It also weakens the K1C as a choice for ABS. The case for the QIDI Q2's 65 °C active heater rests only on QIDI's own claim, because I found no independent measurement of it. So the Q2 pick for engineering filaments stays plausible but is not measured.

That is $112 less than the $789 Bambu X2D AMS Combo, the only other heated-chamber multicolor pair priced in the cited pages.
angles.decides: This supports ChatGPT's choice of the QIDI Q2 for engineering materials and stretches it to shoppers who also want multicolor. At $677 the Q2 + Box costs $112 less than the X2D AMS Combo, and both have a 65 °C heated chamber. The Q2 alone is the same $449 that 3dprintgearlab gives for the P2S, but it adds active heating and about 11% more build volume (18.66 L vs 16.78 L). The P2S stays the pick only for mostly-PLA buyers who want Bambu's ecosystem. The $349 Q2C has the same build volume, but its store listing does not name the heater, so it is not a substitute for ABS/ASA.

Neither gives a flash's output, its full-power flashes per charge or its cost per flash. This page compares watt-seconds, flash count, light per charge and price across the four Godox round-head flashes that take the dome directly. None of them is a product we list or an approved brand, and Amazon blocked amzcheck, so the page has no earning link.

Shop tables list it as '92' or '76' next to the TT685 II's '60' without units or zoom settings, and '76' is the V1's flash energy in watt-seconds (76 Ws), not a guide number.

For long-range direct flash, a 200 mm zoom head is the comparison to make, and I could not put both flashes at the same zoom setting from an opened page.

angles.decides: A dome diffuser costs light, so a flash with more power per pop helps. The V100 gives about 0.4 stop more per pop (log2(100/76) = 0.40) for $20 more, but it delivers 100 fewer full-power flashes per charge (400 vs 500), recycles slower (1.7 s vs 1.3 s) and weighs 616 g with its battery. For event shooting with a dome, the V1Pro stays the pick: more pops, faster recycle, lower cost per flash. The V100 is the pick only if the shopper bounces off high ceilings or uses the larger AK-R22 dome and needs the extra 0.4 stop.

angles.decides: The answer holds: a Godox round-head flash plus the magnetic dome is the simplest diffuser setup, because the dome mounts with no adapter. Godox names the V1 (C/N/S/F/O/P) and the V1 mid (C/N/S/F/O) as round-head flashes for its AK-R1 accessories. The newer V1 mid is the current option for Canon, Nikon, Sony, Fujifilm and Olympus/OM bodies. Panasonic users should pick the V1-P. A TT685II or V860III owner needs the separate S-R1 adapter before any round dome will fit. ChatGPT asked 'What camera do you use?', and the camera brand is what decides which flash version to buy.

angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that a flash only widens its zoom for a dome if it can detect the dome: Nikon's SB-5000 senses its own Diffusion Dome and sets the zoom head to 12, 14 or 17 mm on FX (8, 10 or 11 mm on DX). The Godox V1 manual says nothing about detecting accessories, and its zoom only goes down to 28 mm.
angles.decides: This confirms how the plan works more than it changes the pick. A dome only softens light by spreading it wide and bouncing it off nearby surfaces. Nikon's own manual pairs the dome with bounce flash ('can be further diffused during bounce flash photography') and says the flash zooms to its widest setting by itself when the dome is fitted. On a Godox V1 with an AK-R11, the flash doesn't do this, so the shopper should set the zoom to 28 mm with the ZOOM button and point the head up or to the side. If they leave auto zoom on, the flash follows the lens focal length and sends a narrower beam into the dome. For a shopper who wants it to just work, a system flash that ships with its own dome and senses it (the Nikon SB-5000 with its SW-15H) is the hands-off choice. A Godox V1 plus AK-R11 does the same job at much lower cost but needs that manual step.

pages.why_used: BatteryTrail tabulates 100 A continuous for five brands and ExploringOffGrid says a 100 A BMS is about 1,280 W, but neither names a Group 24 100Ah battery with a 150 A BMS, neither lists Vatrer or Redodo, and neither converts the amp rating into the inverter size one battery can carry. This page does all three with maker-page figures dated today.

None of them explains that using the mic over standard Bluetooth on a computer switches a headset to mono hands-free audio, that the Sony WH-1000XM6's cable turns off Bluetooth so the headset can't take a call, or that Bose added USB-C PC calls only in firmware 8.2.20. Among the budget options, the Soundcore Space 2 Pro (which Dealectric lists) is the only Soundcore model whose US page states a talk time: 20 h, against 30 h of music with ANC on. The Space Q45 that ChatGPT showed states no talk time and is listed as out of stock on Soundcore's US store. Every rated talk time here is at least 20 h, so any of them covers a single workday of calls. The finding changes which one wins on longevity across several days of calls, not whether one makes it through a day.

pages.why_used: I opened the ranked guides: ProjectorVerdict (both pages), iTechGuides, Austin Gallery and Projector Reviews. None turns projector lumens, screen area and gain into a brightness figure, and none says how large a screen a 200–450-lumen portable projector can light. Wirecutter, read through a reader copy, gives only a percentage brightness loss for one budget screen. Esquire blocked the fetch, so I could not check it. This page uses Elite's foot-lambert formula and the SMPTE 16 fL target to give the lumens each screen needs and the screen size that suits each projector.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got turns the screens' advertised diagonals into the picture you actually get for a 16:9 movie. By Elite Screens' own conversion, a square-format Tripod screen sold as 113 inches shows a 92-inch 16:9 picture (80 × 45 in). That is smaller than the 105-inch Yard Master 2, whose 16:9 surface is about 91.5 × 51.5 in, roughly 24% less picture area.
angles.decides: This backs the Yard Master 2 as the movie pick. Elite's 1:1 and 4:3 Tripod sizes are measured across a square or 4:3 surface, so a 16:9 movie fills about 80 × 45 in of a '100"' 4:3 or '113"' 1:1 Tripod, which works out to 92 inches. The Yard Master 2's 1.3-gain CineWhite UHD-B is also brighter than the Tripod's 1.1-gain MaxWhite 2. Anyone buying a Tripod for movies should choose a 16:9 Tripod model (60"–120"), not the 1:1 or 4:3 ones that ChatGPT's 'Best for presentations' card covers. The Aurzen 120" (1.1 gain, 16:9, $24.99) is the low-cost way to get a picture bigger than 100 inches, but stock pages don't say whether it includes a stand.

angles.name: Mechanism
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got works out how bright the picture will be. The rule (from Elite Screens' own article) is foot-lamberts = projector ANSI lumens ÷ screen area in sq ft × gain, with SMPTE 196M's minimum of 12 fL and ideal of 16 fL in a dark room. By that math, a 200-ANSI-lumen portable projector like the Aurzen EAZZE D1G gives only about 5 fL on a 120-inch, 1.1-gain portable screen. That projector reaches 16 fL only at about 68 inches, and a 120-inch, 1.1-gain screen needs about 620 lumens to get there.
angles.decides: The finding sets the screen size and favours higher gain rather than naming one product. ChatGPT's default advice of 100–120 inches only works with a projector of about 400–620 ANSI lumens. A shopper with a 200–300-lumen portable projector should buy about 70–80 inches, or accept a dim picture. At the same size and lumens, the Yard Master 2's 1.3 gain gives 18% more brightness than the 1.1-gain Elite Tripod and Aurzen screens (1.3 ÷ 1.1). So it is the better pick of ChatGPT's choices when the projector is dim, as long as it is sized down.

Wirecutter says the same about the XGIMI portable screen ChatGPT listed as 'best for travel', though without a number. So for picture quality, the tensioned Yard Master 2 is backed by measurements. The Lihong pull-up stays the pick for fast setup on Wirecutter's 10-second time. pages.query: which portable power station can be a ups for a nas and send a usb shutdown signal
pages.why_used: The cited rivals cover NUT 2.8.3, the usbhid-ups driver and the RIVER 3 Plus low-battery bug, but none says EcoFlow's USB link cannot switch the station's AC off and back on after the NAS shuts down (NUT #2735: 'Shutdown does nothing', AC live 60+ s), so the NAS stays off after a short outage. None says EcoFlow's Power Manager lists only the RIVER 3 Plus, or that EcoFlow's Synology package needs port and device-name edits. This page puts those findings in the table and gives a separate pick for each segment, including a UPS that does restart the NAS (UGREEN US3000).

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that stock Synology DSM 7.3.2 does not see an EcoFlow RIVER 3 Plus as a USB UPS (it shows "No USB UPS Connected"). It only works through EcoFlow's Power Manager NAS package, after hand-editing its port (3496 to 3493) and device name (nutdev1 to ups) and switching DSM to Synology UPS Server mode. Even then, several owners report that the NAS never shut down. So "NUT 2.8.3+ support" means support for anyone who runs current NUT, not for the NAS firmware people actually have.
angles.decides: It confirms that no portable power station is a plug-and-play USB UPS for a Synology or QNAP on stock firmware. The RIVER 3 Plus and DELTA 3 Plus only make sense if the NAS can run current NUT itself (2.8.3 or later, which on Debian means forky or sid, not Debian 12 or 13) or can poll a separate NUT server. For a Synology or QNAP owner who wants an automatic shutdown, the pick is a conventional USB HID UPS (APC BE600M1, CyberPower CP1500PFCLCD). The EcoFlow is then a long-runtime source that you shut down on a timer, not one that sends a low-battery signal.

angles.name: Derive
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got works out the cost of adding NAS runtime while keeping the USB shutdown link. EcoFlow's DELTA 3 Series Smart Extra Battery adds 1,024 Wh for $388 ($0.38/Wh). The RIVER 3 Plus EB300 adds 286 Wh for $149 ($0.52/Wh), and the RIVER 3 Plus stops at 858 Wh. Measured DELTA 3 Plus output is 910 Wh per 1,024 Wh, so DELTA 3 Plus plus one extra battery gives about 57 h on a 32 W 2-bay NAS and about 31 h on a 59 W 4-bay NAS.
angles.decides: The USB shutdown requirement leaves only EcoFlow units with a data port: RIVER 3 Plus (USB-B), DELTA 3 Plus (USB-C) and DELTA 3 Ultra / Ultra Plus (USB-C UPS-HID). Among those, the pick depends on how many NAS hours you need. Up to a few hours: RIVER 3 Plus. Overnight or more: DELTA 3 Plus, adding the $388 extra battery if needed. That costs less per added Wh than stacking RIVER 3 Plus EB300s, and the RIVER 3 Plus tops out at 858 Wh. If you need 2 days or more on a 4-bay NAS, the DELTA 3 Ultra at $1,299 for 3,072 Wh ($0.42/Wh nominal) has the lowest cost per hour of any unit with a data port. This supports ChatGPT's RIVER 3 Plus / DELTA 3 Plus split and adds a price-based reason to choose the Ultra.
products: EcoFlow DELTA 3 Plus + DELTA 3 Series Smart Extra Battery
EcoFlow RIVER 3 Plus + EB300 Smart Extra Battery

angles.name: Compatibility
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that EcoFlow's USB HID link cannot cut the station's AC output after the NAS shuts down. NUT's open issue #2735 for the RIVER 3 Plus (firmware V1.33.81.61, Oct 2026) says 'Shutdown does nothing' and that the AC output 'stays live for 60+ seconds', so the NAS stays off when mains power returns. Nor does any result state that EcoFlow's own Power Manager software lists only the RIVER 3 Plus as a supported device, which leaves the DELTA 3 Plus and DELTA 3 Ultra without it.
angles.decides: This confirms the RIVER 3 Plus as the only power station with a maker-documented NAS shutdown path: EcoFlow names it as the only device Power Manager supports, and the cable is in the box. It also limits what the RIVER 3 Plus can do. It can tell a NAS to shut down, but it cannot switch its AC off and back on, so the NAS will not restart by itself after an outage. DSM also needs manual config edits, and commenters on a DS920+ report it hanging instead of shutting down. Shoppers who need unattended recovery should get a conventional USB HID UPS (APC BE600M1 or CyberPower CP1500PFCLCD) or UGREEN's US3000 for NASync. The DELTA 3 Plus and DELTA 3 Ultra only work through generic NUT 2.8.3 or later, without EcoFlow software.

angles.name: Mechanism
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the EcoFlow RIVER 3 Plus and DELTA 3 Plus give NUT no command to switch their AC output off and back on (no load.off, load.off.delay or shutdown.return), so after the NAS shuts itself down the station keeps its outlets live. If mains returns before the battery runs flat, the NAS never sees a power loss and stays off until someone presses its power button.
angles.decides: This confirms the RIVER 3 Plus and DELTA 3 Plus as the only stations here that can signal a shutdown, but it adds a limit to the pick. They can shut a NAS down cleanly, yet they cannot bring it back by themselves after a short outage, because the 'restart after power failure' setting only fires when the NAS really loses power. A NAS the shopper needs to reach remotely, such as one serving a VPN, will stay off. Two things avoid that: a conventional HID UPS (the APC class), which exposes load-off-with-delay commands, or a timer or Wake-on-LAN workaround. The table's 'What a NAS sees' column should add 'won't power the NAS back on after a short outage'.

pages.query: which power station runs a starlink mini and a macbook for a remote workday off grid and for how many days
pages.why_used: The cited pages size this setup from Starlink's 25–40 W rating, a MacBook figure that is assumed rather than measured, and a flat 85% efficiency factor, so they land at 450 Wh a day and about 1.9 days per kWh. None uses the Mini's measured 21 W (Wirelessmoves), the MacBook Air's measured 3.3 W (Notebookcheck) or a station's tested low-load efficiency (techreviewer.de, 80%). This page does, and gets 195 Wh a day and 4.2 workdays from a 1 kWh station. It also checks which ports really carry 20 V/5 A to both devices.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that a power station's "2× USB-C" can mean very different things for this setup. Starlink says the Mini needs a 100 W (20 V/5 A) USB-C PD supply. A Jackery retailer page lists the Explorer 1000 v2's ports as 1 × 100 W + 1 × 30 W, so only one port can run the Mini and the MacBook gets 30 W at most from USB-C. The Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2 lists a 140 W (28 V/5 A) USB-C port and a separate small USB-C1 that shares 20 W with USB-A.
angles.decides: Among the 1 kWh picks ChatGPT showed (Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2, Jackery Explorer 1000 v2, Anker C1000), the Jackery can run the Mini or a MacBook Pro from USB-C, not both at full power. The second laptop has to use the inverter or the 12 V car port with an adapter, and the inverter's idle draw lowers runtime (kilohour assumes 10 W for AC versus 2 W for DC). On listed ports, the Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2 is the better 1 kWh pick for an all-USB-C workday. Days per charge barely change: OutdoorGearLab measured 910 Wh usable from the Jackery's 1,070 Wh, about the same as the 85% derate ChatGPT used. The footnote on cycle life also favours Anker and BLUETTI: the same '4,000 cycles' is claimed to 80% by Anker and BLUETTI but to 70% by Jackery.

angles.name: Derive
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that, using measured inputs (Starlink Mini about 21 W average per Wirelessmoves, MacBook Air M4 about 3.3 W in Notebookcheck's 150-nit Wi-Fi test, and BLUETTI Elite 100 V2 at about 80% usable at double-digit-watt loads per techreviewer.de), one 8-hour workday uses about 195 Wh and a 1,024 Wh station lasts about 4.2 workdays, not the 1.9 days ChatGPT gave.
angles.decides: The days are shorter than the rated figure suggests, because the station loses more at low loads. The light-day load is also about half what ChatGPT assumed. So a 1 kWh LiFePO4 station with two 20 V/5 A USB-C ports (BLUETTI Elite 100 V2, $499, 25 lb) covers about 4 light workdays, or about 2 at the worst case (Mini at 40 W, MacBook at max brightness). That makes the 2 kWh, 40–52 lb class ChatGPT suggested for 'multi-day' unnecessary unless the dish runs 24 h (about 1.5 days per charge). A 200 W kit panel refills a light day in about 1 h at its nameplate output.

angles.name: Compatibility
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got says that the Starlink Mini can run from a power station's 12 V car outlet through Starlink's own Mini Car Adapter (12–24 V in, 60 W out), which leaves the station's one full-power USB-C port free for the MacBook. Anker's US spec table for the SOLIX C1000 Gen 2 gives the 20V/5A, 140 W rating only to USB-C 2 and puts USB-C 1 in a 20 W total shared with USB-A, so on that station the Mini and the MacBook can't both run from USB-C.
angles.decides: This confirms the C1000 Gen 2 as a 1 kWh pick but changes how it gets wired. If USB-C 1 really is capped at 20 W, the MacBook takes the 140 W USB-C 2 and the Mini goes on the 12V/10A (120 W) car outlet through the Starlink Mini Car Adapter. That avoids the AC inverter, which is the efficiency point ChatGPT raised without saying how. Our current page cell 'C1000 Gen 2: 2× 140 W' disagrees with Anker's US spec table and needs fixing. Rule for every candidate: the station needs either two USB-C ports that each offer 20V/5A at the same time, or one such port plus a 12 V car outlet rated about 60 W or more for the Mini Car Adapter.

angles.name: Mechanism
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2, ChatGPT's top pick, has only one USB-C port that can supply the Starlink Mini's required 100 W (20 V/5 A) contract. Anker's own spec table gives USB-C 2 140 W max, while USB-C1 shares 20 W max with USB-A. So ChatGPT's advice to run both the MacBook and the Mini from USB-C does not work on that station. One of them has to go on the 120 W 12 V car socket or on the AC inverter.
angles.decides: It doesn't remove the C1000 Gen 2, but it changes how the page tells you to wire it, and it favors stations with two 100 W USB-C ports for an all-DC setup. On the C1000 Gen 2, put the MacBook on USB-C 2 (up to 140 W) and the Mini on the 12 V/10 A (120 W) car socket through the Mini's 12–48 V DC barrel input. The other option is the Mini on USB-C 2 and the MacBook's charger on AC, which costs inverter losses and cuts the days. Our page's 'USB-C: 2× 140 W' cell for the C1000 Gen 2 contradicts Anker's spec table and must be fixed. The BLUETTI Elite 200 V2 and AC200L rows claim 2× 100 W USB-C. If that holds today, they run both devices on DC with no inverter. That favors them for multi-day trips, but this session didn't confirm it from the maker.

angles.name: Named measurements
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states a measured figure for the power station's own drain: The Technology Man measured the Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2 losing 20% of its charge in 12 hours with the AC inverter on and nothing plugged in (about 17 W). With only the DC side on, the charge stayed at 100%. Over an 8-hour workday that inverter drain adds about 136 Wh to a Starlink Mini plus MacBook Air load of about 320 Wh, and the measured draws (Mini about 21 W, MacBook Air M4 8.7 to 29.9 W) are well below the 450 Wh a day ChatGPT planned for.
angles.decides: The measurements support powering everything from DC and USB-C and switching the inverter off. Measured usable capacities in the 1 kWh class sit close together (Anker C1000 Gen 2: 850–907 Wh on AC and 844 Wh on DC; Jackery 1000 v2: 910 Wh; BLUETTI AC180: 950–983 Wh; EcoFlow DELTA 3 Plus: 910 Wh). The inverter idle drain (about 14–17 W) changes the result more than which station you buy. On DC, 844 Wh ÷ about 320 Wh a day is about 2.6 workdays for the Anker C1000 Gen 2. Running through the inverter adds about 136 Wh a day, so roughly 850 ÷ 456 is about 1.9 days, which happens to be ChatGPT's own figure. That favours a station with two 100 W+ USB-C ports, such as the Anker C1000 Gen 2 (2× 140 W, per our page) or the BLUETTI Elite 200 V2 (2× 100 W), so the Mini and the MacBook both avoid the inverter. The AC180 has only one 100 W USB-C port (per our page), so the second device would have to go through AC or 12 V. For multiple days, StorageReview measured 1.91 kWh out of the Elite 200 V2, about 6 workdays at 320 Wh by the same arithmetic.

pages.query: power station to keep reptile heat on in a power outage
pages.why_used: The cited reptile-outage pages (animalstart.com, pets.co.uk) give only a 'Wh ÷ watts' formula and name no station figures, and the runtime tables built from them use a flat 85% factor with no idle draw. This page gives each station's measured idle draw (9.5–27 W) and delivered Wh. With a 24–50 W reptile heater that idle draw roughly halves the runtime, and it reorders same-size stations: about 56 h vs about 32 h on a 24 W mat for two 2 kWh units.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states how much power the station draws for itself while it waits. Jackery lists 18 W standby for the Explorer 1000 v2, and The Gadgeteer gives about 10 W idle for the BLUETTI Elite 200 V2. A 24 W heat mat draws about as much as that idle load, so the 1,000 Wh class lasts far less time than its Wh rating suggests.
angles.decides: For low-watt reptile heat (heat mats, and emitters cycling on a thermostat), the station's own draw matters as much as its Wh. On a 24 W mat, the Explorer 1000 v2's listed 18 W standby makes it use 42 W in total, so it runs at most about 25 h, not the 38 h that ChatGPT's method gives. The Elite 200 V2 stays the long-outage pick: about 10 W idle per The Gadgeteer and 1.91 kWh delivered in StorageReview's test, so about 56 h on the same mat. The page should give runtimes as Wh ÷ (heater W + idle W), not Wh × 0.85 ÷ heater W. It should also tell owners to turn off BLUETTI's ECO mode. BLUETTI says ECO turns outputs on and off by itself, and that is a risk when a thermostat drops the load to near zero.

angles.name: Derive
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states how much of a small reptile heater's runtime goes to the station's own draw. Jackery lists 18 W standby on the Explorer 1000 v2 and Gidon at The Technology Man measured about 17 W on the Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2, so with a 24 W heat mat about 43% of the battery heats nothing (18 / (24 + 18)). BLUETTI lists 4.5 W standby on the Elite 30 V2. Anker's default Smart AC mode also turns the inverter off after 15 minutes below 20 W, which would cut a thermostat-cycled emitter during its off period.
angles.decides: For a low-watt mat or a thermostat-cycled emitter, standby draw changes the ranking more than capacity does at the small end. The 288 Wh Elite 30 V2, at its stated 4.5 W, runs a 24 W mat about 8.6 h, against about 5.8 h if it drew 18 W like the Jackery. On 1 kWh stations the Anker C1000 Gen 2 (907 Wh measured, 17 W idle) and the Jackery 1000 v2 (1,070 Wh, 18 W standby) both come to about 22 h on a 24 W mat. The pick should say to turn off Anker's Smart AC mode (and the equivalent auto-off on any station) before relying on it with a thermostat. It also confirms the Elite 30 V2 only as a small-mat station.

angles.name: Compatibility
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the BLUETTI AC180 has an ECO mode that switches its outlets off on its own, or that a heater cycled by a thermostat sits at 0 W for long stretches, which is the kind of low load these auto-off modes look for.
angles.decides: This doesn't change which station to buy. Every candidate checked has a 20 ms class transfer and some auto-off, so the finding becomes a setup step on the pick rather than a reason to choose one over another. Before trusting a heater on a thermostat to the AC180 or Explorer 1000 v2, turn off the low-load auto-off (BLUETTI ECO mode, Jackery Energy Saving Mode). Both makers document that you can. Neither unit's UPS is a 0 ms UPS (Jackery's own wording), so a thermostat or controller that reboots on a 20 ms dropout needs testing on the unit.

angles.name: Mechanism
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got says that a power station's own power-saving switch-off (BLUETTI ECO mode, EcoFlow AC timeout, Jackery Energy Saving Mode) cuts the AC outlet when the load stays low or comes and goes. A thermostat that cycles a reptile heater, or a small heat mat, is exactly that kind of load, so the heat can go off partway through an outage unless the owner turns the feature off before the power fails.
angles.decides: This doesn't knock any candidate out, because BLUETTI, EcoFlow and Jackery all let you turn the feature off. It decides whether the plan works at all, so the page needs a 'before the outage: turn off ECO / set AC timeout to Never' step for each pick. It also changes the runtime table. Each station's own draw (AC180 about 15 W per BLUETTI's manual; Jackery 1000 v2 18 W standby per Jackery) is close to a 24 W heat mat's own draw, so the 'heat mat' runtimes are roughly 40% too long. Example: Elite 200 V2 at 2,073.6 Wh × 0.85 ÷ 24 W ≈ 73 h, but ÷ (24 + 15) W ≈ 45 h. That 15 W is the AC180's figure applied to the Elite as an illustration; I didn't find the Elite's own number. Small mats favour stations with a low or adjustable ECO threshold and low idle draw.

angles.name: Named measurements
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states a measured figure for how much power a station uses with its AC outlet on and nothing plugged in. With a 24–50 W reptile heater, that draw cuts runtime far more than ChatGPT's flat 85% efficiency assumes. The Technology Man measured about 19 W on the BLUETTI Elite 30 V2. The Solar Lab measured 16 W on the Elite 100 V2 and 9.5 W on the Elite 200 V2, plus 94% efficiency on the Elite 200 V2.
angles.decides: This confirms the BLUETTI Elite 200 V2 as the pick for multi-day heat. It had the lowest measured idle draw (9.5 W, The Solar Lab) and the highest measured efficiency (94%, The Solar Lab; above 93%, about 2,000 Wh, The Gadgeteer). By my arithmetic it keeps a 24 W mat going for roughly 2,073.6 × 0.93 ÷ (24 + 9.5) ≈ 57 h. It also demotes the 288–300 Wh units (Elite 30 V2, Tenergy T320) to 'a few hours only'. The Technology Man measured about 19 W of AC idle on the Elite 30 V2 with Eco mode off, and only 231 Wh usable on AC. That gives at most 288 ÷ (24 + 19) ≈ 6.7 h for a 24 W mat, the bottom-to-middle of our page's 'About 6–8 h', and about 288 ÷ (50 + 19) ≈ 4.2 h for a 100 W emitter at half duty. Shoppers should also be told to turn off Eco/auto-off for AC: it cuts idle draw but can shut the outlet off while the thermostat has the heater switched off. For the 1 kWh class, The Solar Lab's 16 W idle on the Elite 100 V2 limits a 24 W mat to about 1,024 ÷ (24 + 16) ≈ 25.6 h. That supports 'about a day' as an upper bound, not a typical figure.

The extra runtime costs no more per Wh, so the DELTA 3 Max ($879) or our Elite 200 V2 ($899, $20 more for 25.6 Wh more) beats buying 1 kWh. The DELTA 2 Max loses outright: same 2,048 Wh for $150 more. The 288 Wh class (Elite 30 V2) only makes sense for a small heat mat. pages.query: can a portable power station run a gas furnace during a power outage and how do you connect it
pages.why_used: Outage Authority (cited) gives per-model furnace hours and a stale $/rated-Wh ranking (Elite 200 V2 at $1,399; it is $899 today), and no rival states how many 8-hour furnace nights one charge holds, what each station costs per usable Wh, or that the Elite 200 V2 + 200 W kit costs the same $1,199 as the bare Elite 300 while holding 45% less usable energy and refilling one night only after about 11 hours of full-rated sun.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that BLUETTI's '4,800 W lifting' / '3,900 W Power Lifting' and EcoFlow's '2,200 W X-Boost' headline numbers are resistive-only modes that do not count toward starting a furnace blower motor, and that BLUETTI's Elite 300 and Elite 200 V2 US pages publish no true surge rating at all, while EcoFlow, Jackery and ALLPOWERS publish surge and boost as separate numbers.
angles.decides: A PSC blower needs roughly 1,350–1,800 W to start (PreparedStates quoting DTE), so for 2,400 W-and-up stations (Elite 300, Elite 200 V2, DELTA 3 Max Plus, R4000) the continuous rating alone covers the start and the missing or resistive-only boost number changes nothing; it confirms the 2,400 W+ picks. For 1,800 W-class units (AC180, Elite 100 V2, DELTA 3 Plus) the shopper must not read 'Power Lifting 2,700 W' or 'X-Boost 2,200 W' as surge headroom; only a published true surge (Jackery 1000 v2 3,000 W per Outage Authority; DELTA 3 Plus not confirmed on the maker page today) counts, which keeps the AC180's 'PSC start unverified' flag and argues for the EcoFlow/Jackery units in that class.

angles.name: Derive

The $899 Elite 200 V2 is the value pick per usable Wh ($0.51) if 0.8 of a mild night is enough; the ALLPOWERS R4000 ($0.51 per usable Wh, 1.3 nights) is sold out today.

pages.query: power station to run a pellet smoker overnight
pages.why_used: Traeger's support page gives the D2's 0.08–0.17 A running draw but never mentions power stations. None of the other pages says that the stations shoppers are steered to switch their AC off by themselves at low load: Jackery's Energy Saving Mode is on as shipped and cuts outputs after 12 h, the Anker C1000 Gen 2 cuts after 15 min under 20 W, and the AC180 cuts after 1–4 h under 15–30 W. Any of these can stop a 10–20 W smoker partway through the night. This page names each station's shut-off rule and the setting to change, and it adds the inverter's own all-night draw to the watt-hours per cook.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the power stations it recommended can switch their AC outlet off by themselves when the load is light, or that a Traeger D2 grill holding temperature draws about 10–20 W. That puts the grill at or below those cut-off levels: the Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2 turns its inverter off after 15 minutes under 20 W by default (The Technology Man), and the BLUETTI Elite 100 V2's Eco mode cuts AC below a 10–40 W level set in the app (New Atlas). Either can stop the auger and fan in the middle of the night unless the setting is turned off.
angles.decides: This mostly adds a required setting rather than ruling a station out. With an Anker C1000 Gen 2, turn off Smart AC Output before an overnight cook. With a BLUETTI Elite 100 V2, turn off Eco mode or set the AC level to its 10 W minimum. Otherwise a D2 Traeger idling at about 10–20 W can lose power and the fire goes out. It also shrinks capacity: The Technology Man measured about 17 W inverter overhead on the C1000 Gen 2, which is roughly 200 Wh over 12 hours, as much as the grill uses. That backs the 1 kWh minimum and makes the 2 kWh Elite 200 V2 safer for 12-hour or cold-night cooks.

angles.name: Derive
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the power station's own AC inverter keeps drawing about 10–16 W all night (The Gadgeteer: 10 W on the Elite 200 V2; The Solar Lab: about 16 W on the Elite 100 V2). Against a measured 35 W smoker, that adds 29–46% to an overnight cook. A 12-hour cook then takes about 540–612 Wh from the battery, not the 420 Wh the smoker itself uses. So a 1 kWh station covers about 1.7 overnight cooks and the 2 kWh Elite 200 V2 covers about 3.7.
angles.decides: It confirms that 1 kWh is the minimum for one 12-hour night. The Elite 100 V2 runs one night with about 400 Wh left, not the 2+ nights that 0.85-derate arithmetic suggests. It also argues for the Elite 200 V2 when the shopper wants two back-to-back nights without recharging, and it costs less per overnight cook. Our table's '1' for 1 kWh units stands. For the Elite 200 V2, the sourced arithmetic gives about 3.7 rather than 2–3.

angles.name: Compatibility
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the BLUETTI AC180's ECO mode turns its AC outlets off when the load stays under a set 15–30 W for 1–4 hours, or that a Traeger D2 grill draws only about 10–20 W once it is up to temperature (0.08–0.17 A at 120 V, per Traeger), so with ECO on the outlet can switch off and the fire goes out mid-cook.
angles.decides: This doesn't change capacity sizing (about 1 kWh still fits a 12-hour cook). It adds a required setup step and a comparison column. On any BLUETTI unit, ECO must be off before an overnight cook, because a D2 Traeger idling at about 10–20 W sits below the AC180's lowest selectable 15–30 W cutoff. Anker's C1000 outlets shut off only when no plug is detected for 15 minutes, with no wattage rule, so a plugged-in grill keeps power. That makes the Anker C1000 (the card ChatGPT showed at $449.99) the safer choice if the shopper won't change settings. Anker's −20 °C to 40 °C discharge range also covers a cold overnight cook.

angles.name: Mechanism
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that a Traeger D2 grill holding temperature draws only 0.08–0.17 A (about 10–20 W at 120 V). That sits inside the low-load window where the BLUETTI AC180's ECO mode switches AC off after 1–4 hours. The Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 ships with Energy Saving Mode on and turns all outputs off after 12 hours at low load. Either can kill the grill partway through the night.
angles.decides: This finding confirms the plan works rather than changing the pick. Any 1 kWh-class LiFePO4 unit already listed has enough energy. For an overnight cook, the page needs one setup step: turn off AC ECO on the BLUETTI AC180 (app or setting mode) and Energy Saving Mode on the Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 before lighting the grill, or the AC can shut off unattended. A Traeger power-loss shutdown leaves the fire out until someone restarts it. The finding also argues against relying on the 25–30 W auto-off defaults with low-draw D2 or WiFIRE grills. It does not by itself rank one station above another.

angles.name: Named measurements
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states a named, measured energy use for a whole pellet-smoker cook on battery: Mike Sokol (RVelectricity) ran a Z Grills smoker from a Jackery Explorer 1000 and measured about 194 W at ignition, 35 W while running and 0.21 kWh (210 Wh) over a 6-hour rib cook. Applied to a 12-hour overnight cook, that is about 420 Wh. Reviewer-measured usable output of 850–910 Wh from the 1 kWh stations covers that about twice, but only if the inverter's own draw stays small.
angles.decides: This confirms a roughly 1 kWh LiFePO4 station as the pick and shows ChatGPT's 'at least 500 Wh' floor and 200–400 W startup band are about right. The measured 35 W × 12 h = 420 Wh, plus a few Wh for ignition. That is less than half of the usable output reviewers measured: Notebookcheck got 850 Wh from the Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2 and OutdoorGearLab got 910 Wh from the Jackery Explorer 1000 v2. So 'cooks per charge' for the 1 kWh rows could read 2, not 1. The catch is inverter self-consumption. If it is around 15 W (New Atlas, for the BLUETTI AC180, without saying whether it was measured), it adds about 180 Wh per 12 hours and pushes a 1 kWh unit back toward 1–1.5 cooks. That makes idle draw the figure that decides between the 1 kWh rows. The BLUETTI Elite 30 V2 is ruled out for a 12-hour cook on arithmetic alone: 420 Wh is more than its rated 288 Wh before any losses. The measured 194 W ignition peak is well within its 600 W AC output, so it would only cover roughly a 6–7 hour cook.

pages.why_used: Every cited Soundcore page gives the AeroClip 2's 8 h/32 h and the C50i's 7 h/28 h with no codec or volume conditions, and none says the C50i also plays LDAC. Soundcore's own support tables show that with LDAC on, the AeroClip 2 falls to 5 h at 50% volume (3 h at 100%) and the C50i drops multipoint. This page is the only one with that fully maker-sourced battery and codec fact, which removes LDAC and battery as reasons to pay for the AeroClip 2 and leaves the call microphones as the reason.

Soundcore's own C50i FAQ also lists LDAC (SBC/AAC/LDAC) and says dual connection is off while LDAC is on, so LDAC does not set the AeroClip 2 apart.
angles.decides: This confirms the C50i as the pick for music and everyday use and narrows the AeroClip 2 case to calls only. Both ChatGPT answers that give winners credit the AeroClip 2 for music partly because of LDAC, and the table one gives it a 'modest' battery win. Soundcore's own figures say the C50i also does LDAC. With LDAC on, the AeroClip 2 runs 5 h at 50% volume against the C50i's 7 h (the C50i figure is at Soundcore's standard test codec, not LDAC). In call mode, the gap is 5 h (AeroClip 2) vs 4.5 h (C50i). The AeroClip 2's real edge stays the 4 mics + 2 VPU call pickup and the 10 min = 4 h fast charge (vs 2 h). That is what the $100 gap at list price ($169.99 vs $69.99 on us.soundcore.com) pays for.

pages.query: is a thunderbolt 5 ssd enclosure worth it for a macbook pro m4 and which one
pages.why_used: The cited ACASIS pages and OWC blog carry only maker claims (over 6,000 MB/s) and DPReview publishes ratios with no MB/s, so none of them shows what each bare enclosure actually measures on a Mac. This page puts named-tester Mac figures for the OWC, UGREEN, ORICO, Satechi and TerraMaster enclosures side by side and exposes the write-speed gap (ORICO about 3,000 MB/s write vs 5,776 to 6,001 MB/s for OWC and UGREEN), which decides the pick.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states what the makers' '80Gbps / up to 6,000–7,061 MB/s' claims shrink to on a Mac in a named tester's hands: every JHL9480 enclosure hangs the SSD on a PCIe 4.0 x4 (64 Gb/s) link, reads land at 6,000–6,500 MB/s, writes range from about 3,000 MB/s (Notebookcheck, ORICO X50 Pro on a TB5 MacBook Pro) to 5,776–6,001 MB/s (Macwelt, OWC 1M2 80G and UGREEN D705), sustained writes fall to about 1.4 GB/s once the SSD's roughly 50 GB SLC cache fills (Eclectic Light), and on a base-M4 Thunderbolt 4 port the same enclosure reads about 3,186 MB/s (TerraMaster's own base M4 Mac mini run).
angles.decides: Splits the answer by chip exactly where the shopper question does. Base M4 MacBook Pro: TerraMaster's own base-M4 Mac mini run (about 3,186 MB/s read) and Eclectic Light's USB4 figure (about 3.4 GB/s) show a TB5 enclosure delivers 40 Gb/s-rung speed there, so it is not worth the premium over a USB4 enclosure. M4 Pro/Max: the claimed read/write numbers are near-identical across enclosures, so the measured Mac write is what separates them: Macwelt measured 6,001 MB/s write on the UGREEN D705 (fan) and 5,776 MB/s on the OWC Express 1M2 80G (one-hour run, minimal throttling), while Notebookcheck measured about 3,000 MB/s write on the ORICO X50 Pro on a TB5 MacBook Pro against a 5,800 MB/s claim. That supports UGREEN or OWC over ORICO for write-heavy work, and the post-cache 1.4 GB/s figure says the SSD's cache size (bigger on 4 TB than 1 TB) matters more than the enclosure for 50 GB+ copies. Caveat: TB5 enclosures accept PCIe 5.0 drives only as compatibility, never for speed; the link is Gen4 x4 in all of them, and Notebookcheck's Gen5 Z540 was not detected in the ORICO at all.
products: UGREEN 80Gbps Thunderbolt 5 M.2 NVMe SSD Enclosure with fan (D705)

angles.name: Derive
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that on a base-M4 MacBook Pro (Thunderbolt 4, 40 Gb/s) a $149–$232 Thunderbolt 5 enclosure reads 1 TB in the same 4 min 23 s as a $54.90 USB4 enclosure, while on an M4 Pro/Max the measured gain is only about 1 min 36 s to 1 min 49 s per TB read, and the ORICO X50 Pro's measured 3,000 MB/s write on a TB5 Mac makes a 1 TB write take 5 min 33 s, slower than the TB4 rung.
angles.decides: Confirms 'no' for a base M4 MacBook Pro: every TB5 enclosure runs at the 3,800 MB/s TB4 rung there, so the $94–$177 premium over a $54.90 USB4 enclosure buys zero seconds. For M4 Pro/Max it narrows the pick: OWC Express 1M2 80G (6,000/5,500 measured) and UGREEN fanless (6,511/6,001 measured) deliver the TB5 gain on both reads and writes, while the ORICO X50 Pro's measured 3,000 MB/s write on a TB5 Mac is no better than USB4 for card offloads. It also undercuts ChatGPT's 'add a 990 Pro' advice: at Samsung's $639.99 for 2 TB, enclosure + drive costs $839.98 versus $749.99 for OWC's own prebuilt 1M2 80G 2 TB.

angles.decides: It confirms ChatGPT's pairing of a PCIe 4.0 Samsung 990 Pro with any of the three enclosures, but adds the decisive exclusions a shopper hits if they already own or plan a Gen 5 drive: with the UGREEN fan model it is unsupported by the maker, with the OWC it must average 11 W or less (OWC names the 9100 Pro as a passing example), and ACASIS is the only one of the three that claims unrestricted native Gen 5 support. It also narrows the pick for anyone who needs to plug the drive into a plain USB 3 port (older Mac, dock, PC): UGREEN says its fan enclosure is not backward compatible with USB 2/3, whereas our page already notes ORICO's X50 Pro and UGREEN's finned model carry a USB fallback controller. Base-M4 buyers get Thunderbolt 4 ports only, so OWC's own figure of up to 3,800 MB/s applies and the TB5 premium is wasted.

angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that Thunderbolt 5's storage gain is a PCIe-tunnel step (Intel: 'double the PCI Express data throughput', built on PCIe Gen 4) that only an M4 Pro/Max port exposes, that OWC's own ladder puts the same 80G enclosure at 'over 6000MB/s' on TB5 but 'up to 3800MB/s' on a TB4 port like the base M4's, that Howard Oakley found full TB5 speed needs macOS 15.3 or later, and that OWC limits PCIe Gen 5 SSDs inside to about 11 W average.

On M4 Pro/Max (Apple: 'Thunderbolt 5 (up to 120Gb/s)') the enclosure reaches 'over 6000MB/s', and Oakley's measured ceiling is about 6 GB/s, so a PCIe 4.0 SSD (990 Pro class) is the right pairing; a PCIe 5.0 SSD adds no bandwidth and OWC warns it must average 11 W or less in the bus-powered 1M2 80G. The shopper must also run macOS 15.3 or later for full TB5 speed. Any TB5 enclosure on an M4 MacBook Pro keeps TRIM and SMART (Oakley: NVMe interface trims; SMART works over Thunderbolt/USB4, not USB 3.x), so that does not separate the candidates.

pages.query: what ups or power station keeps a bambu lab p1s printing through a power flicker or outage
pages.why_used: The cited Bambu forum thread and spec PDFs give P1S wattage. None of them compares switchover times at the same price. This page shows that BLUETTI sells a 10 ms station (Elite 100 V2) for the same $499 as the 20 ms AC180. It gives every candidate's rated or lab-measured switchover time and turns each battery into P1S printing hours at the measured 130 W. Separately, the angle-C agent reported that the live page has text addressed to AI assistants (an instruction to show an AC180 card). This rewrite has none of it, and that text should be removed from the live page.

angles.name: Normalise
angles.gap: None of the results ChatGPT got says that BLUETTI's own US store sells the Elite 100 V2 (1,024 Wh, '10ms UPS Backup') at the same $499 as the AC180 that ChatGPT showed as a card, whose switchover BLUETTI states as 20 ms. So at the same price, one station switches over in half the time the other does.
angles.decides: For keeping a P1S printing through a flicker, switchover time is the spec that matters, and a shorter one gives more margin. A 1 kWh station at $499 is now available from BLUETTI with a 10 ms rating (Elite 100 V2) instead of 20 ms (AC180). That makes the Elite 100 V2 the better 1 kWh pick at the same price. The AC180 drops to second place, because it has 128 Wh more capacity but a switchover twice as long. The CyberPower CP1500PFCLCD (4 ms typical) is still the safest pick for flickers only. Its vendor figures work out to about 83 Wh delivered at 500 W, roughly a twelfth of a 1 kWh station, so it is not a choice for riding out an outage. No published test shows a P1S rebooting on a 20 ms transfer, so the page should present this as spec margin, not as proven failure.

angles.name: Derive
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states what an hour of P1S backup costs per station: at the 100–130 W a 120 V P1S draws once warm (holmes4's measurement), the BLUETTI AC180 ($499, about 7.5 h) and Elite 200 V2 ($899, about 13.6 h) both cost about $66 per printing-hour, while the 288 Wh Elite 30 V2 ($289.99, about 1.9 h) costs about $154.
angles.decides: This confirms a lithium station of 1 kWh or more as the outage pick and makes the choice between them a matter of runtime, not value. The AC180 and Elite 200 V2 both cost about $66 per printing-hour, so buy the Elite 200 V2 only if prints run longer than about 7.5 h, because it covers about 13.6 h, enough for an overnight print. A 288–300 Wh unit costs more than twice as much per hour and lasts under 2 h, so it suits flickers and short outages. Every 600 W station has about 1.7× headroom over the 120 V heat-up peak of about 350 W. The Tenergy T320 (200 W continuous) stays off the list.

angles.name: Compatibility
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that BLUETTI's AC180 manual rates the unit as a UPS at no more than 20 ms and 1,440 W maximum, and only at 10–30 °C (50–86 °F). The same manual tells owners to turn off Grid Enhancement mode when using it as a UPS, because otherwise the switchover slows and may not deliver instant backup power.
angles.decides: This confirms the BLUETTI AC180 as the multi-hour pick for a US P1S. The P1S peak at 120 V (Bambu says 350 W in the ChatGPT-cited spec, which I could not open myself) is well under the 1,440 W UPS limit. It adds two setup conditions to print on the page: turn Grid Enhancement off, and keep the unit at 10–30 °C, which rules out a cold garage. For flickers only, the Elite 30 V2 is the stronger budget pick on paper: ≤10 ms switchover, and 980 W from the wall in UPS mode covers the bed-heating peak with the inverter only needed during an outage. A CyberPower line UPS still works with the P1S on its battery outlets because the P1S is not on the manual's banned list, but the page should say to keep the load under the manual's 80 % guideline.

angles.name: Mechanism
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the P1S's internal 24 V supply is only 108 W and powers everything except the heated bed, which runs straight off the mains. A line flicker or sag therefore reboots the printer through that small supply, and the CyberPower datasheet says its AVR fixes low-voltage sags 'without switching to battery mode'. A forum owner reported P1S printers freezing mid-print during brownouts on an EcoFlow DELTA 2 used as a UPS.
angles.decides: It confirms a line-interactive sine-wave UPS with AVR, such as the CyberPower CP1500PFCLCD, as the pick for flickers. Most flickers are sags rather than full outages, and the AVR raises low voltage without a battery transfer, so the printer's 108 W electronics supply never sees a gap. For long outages, a power station can still go behind or alongside the UPS, but the page should not promise that a power station's UPS mode keeps a P1S running through brownouts, because a P1S owner's DELTA 2 did not. Bed sizing on 120 V stays at the 350 W peak.
products: Bambu Lab X1C (same bed design as P1 series)

angles.name: Named measurements
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states a measured switchover time for any power station. StorageReview timed the switch from wall to battery with a Quarch Mains Power Analysis Module and got 9 ms for the EcoFlow RIVER 3 Plus and just over 8 ms for the EcoFlow DELTA 3 Plus. No measured figure exists for the BLUETTI AC180 (rated 20 ms) or the BLUETTI Elite 200 V2 (rated 15 ms).
angles.decides: This supports the flicker-proof pick among power stations: the only candidates with a lab-measured sub-10 ms switchover are the EcoFlow RIVER 3 Plus (short outages) and the EcoFlow DELTA 3 Plus (long outages). The AC180, Elite 200 V2 and ALLPOWERS units have only maker ratings of 10–20 ms. No one has measured whether a P1S itself rides through a given gap, so a 'test it yourself' line still belongs on the page. StorageReview's measured usable capacities confirm the runtime column roughly. At a 150 W PLA average: AC180 1,030 Wh ≈ 6.9 h (our page says 6.4), Elite 200 V2 1,910 Wh ≈ 12.7 h (page says 11.5), DELTA 3 Plus 910 Wh ≈ 6.1 h.

angles.name: Whole category, priced
angles.gap: No result ChatGPT got states that a LiFePO4 station claiming a ≤10 ms UPS switchover with 980 W pass-through (BLUETTI Elite 30 V2) costs $289.99 on the maker's store, the same money as the 1500 VA lead-acid UPSes it recommended, or that EcoFlow's own store sells the DELTA 3 Classic (same 1,024 Wh, 1,800 W and 10 ms auto-switch claim) at $479, $100 below the $579 DELTA 3 it showed.
angles.decides: This reframes the flicker pick. At the same price as a CyberPower or APC 1500 VA UPS, the Elite 30 V2 claims the same class of switchover (≤10 ms). Its 980 W pass-through covers the P1S's 350 W maximum at 110 V, and it holds about 245 usable Wh (about 1.6 h at 150 W) where the lead-acid UPSes give tens of minutes. For whole-print outages, the 1 kWh pick at the maker's price becomes the DELTA 3 Classic at $479 (10 ms claim) instead of the $579 DELTA 3. The AC180 ($499) and P1800 ($399) are cheaper per Wh, but our page records a 20 ms switchover for both, double the 10 ms claims.
